PLA has dimensional stability, low shrinkage, and is easy to process, allowing accurate prints at lower extrusion temperatures without heated beds or enclosures. However, it suffers from low glass-transition temperature and brittle failure under impact or sustained heat. ABS offers higher impact resistance, superior layer fusion, chemical resistance, and significantly higher heat tolerance due to its higher glass-transition temperature, at the cost of increased warping risk, higher energy input, and the need for controlled thermal environments. Material selection therefore hinges on whether the application favors visual quality, accuracy, and indoor safety (PLA) or functional durability, thermal resilience, and mechanical toughness under real-world loads (ABS). What Are the Main Material Differences Between ABS and PLA for 3D Printing? The main material differences between ABS and PLA for 3D printing are listed below. Printing Temperature : PLA has a lower printing temperature, between 180°C and 220°C, while ABS requires higher temperatures, ranging from 220°C to 250°C. The difference affects the ease of printing, with PLA being easier to print at lower temperatures. Strength and Durability : ABS is stronger and more impact-resistant than PLA. ABS is more flexible and handles higher stress without breaking. PLA is more rigid and brittle, making it less suitable for parts that undergo mechanical stress. Heat Resistance : ABS has better heat resistance, maintaining its shape at higher temperatures (up to 100°C). PLA begins to deform at around 60°C, limiting its use in high-temperature environments. Surface Finish : PLA provides a smoother, shinier finish compared to ABS. ABS is smoothed with acetone to achieve a glossy finish, while PLA’s finish is more consistent. Environmental Impact : PLA is biodegradable and made from renewable resources, making it more environmentally friendly than ABS, which is petroleum-based and not biodegradable. How Do ABS Fumes Compare to PLA Fumes During Printing? ABS fumes are compared to PLA fumes during printing by their chemical compound (styrene). ABS emits styrene, a volatile organic compound that irritates the respiratory system and causes long-term health risks if inhaled in large amounts. PLA produces minimal fumes compared to ABS, mainly consisting of harmless, biodegradable compounds (lactide). ABS requires proper ventilation or an enclosure to minimize exposure to harmful fumes, while PLA is considered safer to print with in non-ventilated spaces. PLA’s fumes pose a much lower health risk compared to the more toxic fumes released by ABS during printing. Using acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS) and poly-lactic acid (PLA) presents a risk of exposure to respirable particles according to “Particle emissions from fused deposition modeling 3D printers: Evaluation and meta-analysis,” written by P Byrley and BJ George on November 12, 2018. PLA is considered safer to print with in indoor environments, as it poses lower health risks than ABS. Which One Is Better for Temperature (Heat) Resistance, PLA vs ABS? ABS is better for temperature (heat) resistance compared to PLA. ABS withstands temperatures up to 100°C without deforming, making it ideal for parts exposed to heat (automotive or appliance components). PLA begins to soften at around 60°C, making it unsuitable for high-temperature applications. ABS’s higher glass transition temperature allows it to maintain its shape and strength under heat, while PLA’s lower heat resistance leads to warping or failure in hot environments. For heat-resistant applications, ABS is far superior in heat resistance, as it bears temperatures up to 100°C or more without losing structural integrity, according to “PLA vs. ABS – Which Is Better?” written by BigRep, published on June 03, 2025. Which Material, ABS or PLA, Offers Better Impact Resistance? ABS offers better impact resistance compared to PLA because of its molecular structure and material properties. ABS is more flexible and withstands higher forces before breaking or cracking. It is used for parts that require durability (protective covers and automotive components). PLA is more brittle and tends to break under stress, making it less suitable for applications requiring high impact resistance. ABS's superior strength and toughness make it the ideal choice for functional parts exposed to mechanical stress. “PLA shows brittle nature when subjected to out-of-plane loading, i.e., impact,” according to “An Investigation Into Low Velocity Impact Of 3D Printed Thermoplastic Plates” written by Guneet Kaur Mankoo, published on October 08, 2021. Which Material Cools and Solidifies More Predictably, PLA or ABS? PLA is the material that cools and solidifies more predictably. PLA has a lower melting point, ranging from 180 to 220°C, and solidifies fast once the print head moves away. Its cooling process is less prone to warping, and the material retains its shape better without the need for additional temperature control. ABS has a higher melting point and tends to shrink and warp as it cools. It makes ABS more challenging to work with for larger prints, as it requires a heated bed and an enclosure to prevent temperature fluctuations that affect the solidification process. Which Material Provides Better Overall Tensile Strength, PLA or ABS? ABS is the material that provides better overall tensile strength. ABS has higher impact resistance and endures more stress before breaking or deforming. It is more flexible, allowing it to absorb forces without fracturing. PLA is more rigid and tends to break under stress, offering lower tensile strength. ABS is ideal for applications where durability and mechanical strength are required (automotive parts or functional components). PLA is more suited for decorative items that do not undergo significant mechanical stress. Which Material Shows Less Warping During Printing, PLA or ABS? PLA is the material that shows less warping during printing. PLA has a lower melting point and solidifies fast, which reduces the likelihood of warping as it cools. ABS tends to shrink more as it cools, leading to higher stress and warping on larger prints. PLA's lower temperature sensitivity makes it easier to print without the need for a heated bed or enclosure, unlike ABS, which requires both to prevent warping. It makes PLA a more reliable material for precise prints and smaller projects. Which Material Delivers Higher Dimensional Accuracy, PLA or ABS? PLA is the material that delivers higher dimensional accuracy. PLA has lower shrinkage during cooling, which results in fewer distortions and better precision in prints. ABS, on the other hand, tends to shrink more as it cools, leading to potential warping and dimensional inaccuracies. PLA's ease of printing without the need for a heated bed ensures that the printed object retains its intended shape and size. ABS requires more careful temperature control to maintain dimensional consistency, making PLA a more reliable material for accurate prints. Which Material Performs Better in Outdoor Environments, PLA or ABS? ABS is the material that performs better in outdoor environments. ABS has higher Ultraviolet (UV) resistance and withstands prolonged exposure to sunlight without degrading. PLA, being biodegradable, breaks down faster when exposed to outdoor elements (sunlight and moisture). ABS maintains its strength and color for a longer period, making it suitable for outdoor applications (automotive parts and garden tools). PLA’s sensitivity to environmental factors makes it more appropriate for indoor use or short-term outdoor projects. Which Material Has Superior Layer Adhesion, PLA or ABS? ABS is the material that has superior layer adhesion. ABS bonds better between layers due to its higher printing temperature and improved layer fusion. The higher extrusion temperature of ABS allows for better adhesion between layers, reducing the likelihood of delamination or layer separation. PLA, with its lower printing temperature, struggles to bond layers as effectively in prints that require strength and durability. ABS’s improved layer adhesion makes it ideal for functional parts that must endure stress and wear. Which Material Produces Stronger Functional Parts, PLA or ABS? ABS is the material that produces stronger functional parts. ABS has higher impact resistance and endures physical stress better than PLA, making it ideal for applications (automotive components or tools). PLA is more rigid but tends to be brittle, breaking under pressure or impact. ABS’s flexibility and durability allow it to withstand wear and tear, while PLA is more suited for decorative or low-stress applications. ABS’s ability to handle mechanical forces and higher temperatures makes it the preferred material for functional parts. Which Material Is More Resistant to Chemicals, PLA or ABS? ABS is a material that is more resistant to chemicals. ABS withstands exposure to a broader range of chemicals (oils, acids, and alkaline solutions) without degradation. PLA is more susceptible to chemical damage and likely breaks down when exposed to certain solvents, oils, or strong acids. For example, ABS is used in environments where chemical exposure is expected (plumbing or automotive parts). PLA’s lower resistance to chemicals limits its use in applications where durability against harsh substances is needed. Which Material Is More Flexible or Less Brittle, PLA or ABS? ABS is a material that is more flexible and less brittle. ABS has better impact resistance and bends without breaking, making it suitable for functional parts that need durability. PLA is more rigid and tends to be brittle, which makes it more likely to crack or break under stress. ABS’s flexibility allows it to absorb shocks and withstand mechanical forces better than PLA, making it more suitable for decorative or low-stress applications. ABS is the preferred choice due to its increased flexibility for parts exposed to regular handling or stress. Which Material Is Safer To Print Indoors, PLA or ABS? PLA is a material that is safer to print indoors. PLA emits fewer harmful fumes during printing, releasing biodegradable compounds (lactide). ABS releases more toxic fumes (styrene), which irritate the respiratory system and require proper ventilation. PLA is less likely to cause health concerns and is more suitable for indoor environments with limited airflow. ABS requires additional precautions (e.g., using an enclosure or ensuring good ventilation) when printing indoors due to its higher emission levels. What Are the Similarities Between PLA and ABS? The similarities between PLA and ABS are listed below. 3D Printing Compatibility : PLA and ABS are used for 3D printing. Each is compatible with consumer-grade 3D printers and is readily available in filament form. Ease of Use: Polylactic Acid and Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene are relatively simple to print with, though ABS requires a heated bed for optimal results. Its moderate printing temperatures make them accessible for general 3D printing applications. Strength and Durability : PLA and ABS offer adequate strength and durability for various printing needs. ABS is more flexible and durable, while PLA is more rigid but is suitable for a range of functional prints. Surface Finishing : PLA and ABS are post-processed to achieve smoother finishes. Sanding, painting, or chemical smoothing is possible with either material to improve the surface quality. What Are the Mutual Alternative 3D Filaments for PLA and ABS? The mutual alternative 3D filaments for PLA and ABS are listed below. Polyethylene Terephthalate Glycol (PETG): PETG is a versatile filament known for its durability, chemical resistance, and ease of use. The alternative combines the strength of ABS with the comfort of printing of PLA, making it a popular alternative. Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU): TPU is a flexible filament with excellent elasticity and abrasion resistance. It is ideal for creating rubber-like prints and is used for phone cases, wearables, and flexible parts. Nylon : Nylon is a strong, durable, and flexible filament that offers great impact resistance and wear properties. It is suitable for functional parts and mechanical applications, but it requires a heated bed to print correctly. Acrylonitrile Styrene Acrylate (ASA): For outdoor applications and parts exposed to the elements, printing ASA can be a strong alternative to ABS because it offers better UV resistance and outdoor durability. High Impact Polystyrene (HIPS): HIPS is used as a support material for ABS prints, but is printed on its own for low-stress applications. It is a good alternative when smooth surface finishes are needed and falls under the types of 3D filaments when considering its applications. ABS’s strength and flexibility make it the preferred choice for mechanical applications, while PLA is more commonly used for decorative or low-stress prints. Does ABS Resist Heat Better Compared to PLA? Yes, ABS resists heat better compared to PLA. ABS is able to withstand higher temperatures, with a heat resistance up to ~85–95 °C, while PLA starts to deform around 60°C. It makes ABS more suitable for applications exposed to heat (automotive parts or appliances). PLA is more sensitive to high temperatures and warps or loses its structural integrity when exposed to heat for prolonged periods. ABS’s superior heat resistance makes it a better option for functional parts that need to endure higher thermal conditions. Is ABS More Durable Compared to PLA? Yes, ABS is more durable compared to PLA. ABS has higher impact resistance and withstands more physical stress without cracking. It is more flexible and less brittle than PLA, making it ideal for parts that are subjected to regular handling or mechanical wear. ABS performs better in high-temperature environments, where PLA softens and loses its structural integrity. For example, ABS is commonly used in automotive parts or functional prototypes, while PLA is more suited for decorative items and low-stress applications. The added durability and heat resistance of ABS make it a better choice for long-lasting and functional parts. Does ABS Warp More Easily Compared to PLA? No, ABS does not warp more easily compared to PLA. ABS is more prone to warping due to its higher printing temperature and tendency to shrink during cooling. PLA, with a lower melting point, experiences less shrinkage and is less likely to warp during printing. ABS requires a heated bed and controlled environment to minimize warping for larger prints. PLA is printed without a heated bed and tends to maintain its shape more easily. The difference in temperature sensitivity and shrinkage characteristics makes PLA a better option for prints that need to avoid warping. Is ABS More Flexible Than PLA? Yes, ABS is more flexible than PLA. ABS has better impact resistance and bends without breaking, making it ideal for functional parts that require durability and flexibility. PLA is more rigid and tends to be brittle, which leads to cracking or breaking under stress. ABS’s flexibility allows it to withstand physical stress better than PLA in applications (automotive parts or tools). PLA’s rigidity, while suitable for decorative and low-stress prints, makes it less ideal for parts that need to endure mechanical forces. Start Your Instant Quote STEP · STP · SLDPRT · STL · DXF · IPT · X_T · X_B · 3DXML · CATPART · PRT · SAT · 3MF · JT Upload Your Design All uploads are secure and confidential PLA and ABS differ fundamentally in thermal behavior, mechanical response, and processing requirements, which drives their distinct use cases in FDM printing. PLA has dimensional stability, low shrinkage, and is easy to process, allowing accurate prints at lower extrusion temperatures without heated beds or enclosures. However, it suffers from low glass-transition temperature and brittle failure under impact or sustained heat. ABS offers higher impact resistance, superior layer fusion, chemical resistance, and significantly higher heat tolerance due to its higher glass-transition temperature, at the cost of increased warping risk, higher energy input, and the need for controlled thermal environments. Material selection therefore hinges on whether the application favors visual quality, accuracy, and indoor safety (PLA) or functional durability, thermal resilience, and mechanical toughness under real-world loads (ABS). What Are the Main Material Differences Between ABS and PLA for 3D Printing? The main material differences between ABS and PLA for 3D printing are listed below. Printing Temperature : PLA has a lower printing temperature, between 180°C and 220°C, while ABS requires higher temperatures, ranging from 220°C to 250°C. The difference affects the ease of printing, with PLA being easier to print at lower temperatures. Strength and Durability : ABS is stronger and more impact-resistant than PLA. ABS is more flexible and handles higher stress without breaking. PLA is more rigid and brittle, making it less suitable for parts that undergo mechanical stress. Heat Resistance : ABS has better heat resistance, maintaining its shape at higher temperatures (up to 100°C). PLA begins to deform at around 60°C, limiting its use in high-temperature environments. Surface Finish : PLA provides a smoother, shinier finish compared to ABS. ABS is smoothed with acetone to achieve a glossy finish, while PLA’s finish is more consistent. Environmental Impact : PLA is biodegradable and made from renewable resources, making it more environmentally friendly than ABS, which is petroleum-based and not biodegradable. How Do ABS Fumes Compare to PLA Fumes During Printing? ABS fumes are compared to PLA fumes during printing by their chemical compound (styrene). ABS emits styrene, a volatile organic compound that irritates the respiratory system and causes long-term health risks if inhaled in large amounts. PLA produces minimal fumes compared to ABS, mainly consisting of harmless, biodegradable compounds (lactide). ABS requires proper ventilation or an enclosure to minimize exposure to harmful fumes, while PLA is considered safer to print with in non-ventilated spaces. PLA’s fumes pose a much lower health risk compared to the more toxic fumes released by ABS during printing. Using acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS) and poly-lactic acid (PLA) presents a risk of exposure to respirable particles according to “Particle emissions from fused deposition modeling 3D printers: Evaluation and meta-analysis,” written by P Byrley and BJ George on November 12, 2018. PLA is considered safer to print with in indoor environments, as it poses lower health risks than ABS. Which One Is Better for Temperature (Heat) Resistance, PLA vs ABS? ABS is better for temperature (heat) resistance compared to PLA. ABS withstands temperatures up to 100°C without deforming, making it ideal for parts exposed to heat (automotive or appliance components). PLA begins to soften at around 60°C, making it unsuitable for high-temperature applications. ABS’s higher glass transition temperature allows it to maintain its shape and strength under heat, while PLA’s lower heat resistance leads to warping or failure in hot environments. For heat-resistant applications, ABS is far superior in heat resistance, as it bears temperatures up to 100°C or more without losing structural integrity, according to “PLA vs. ABS – Which Is Better?” written by BigRep, published on June 03, 2025. Which Material, ABS or PLA, Offers Better Impact Resistance? ABS offers better impact resistance compared to PLA because of its molecular structure and material properties. ABS is more flexible and withstands higher forces before breaking or cracking. It is used for parts that require durability (protective covers and automotive components). PLA is more brittle and tends to break under stress, making it less suitable for applications requiring high impact resistance. ABS's superior strength and toughness make it the ideal choice for functional parts exposed to mechanical stress. “PLA shows brittle nature when subjected to out-of-plane loading, i.e., impact,” according to “An Investigation Into Low Velocity Impact Of 3D Printed Thermoplastic Plates” written by Guneet Kaur Mankoo, published on October 08, 2021. Which Material Cools and Solidifies More Predictably, PLA or ABS? PLA is the material that cools and solidifies more predictably. PLA has a lower melting point, ranging from 180 to 220°C, and solidifies fast once the print head moves away. Its cooling process is less prone to warping, and the material retains its shape better without the need for additional temperature control. ABS has a higher melting point and tends to shrink and warp as it cools. It makes ABS more challenging to work with for larger prints, as it requires a heated bed and an enclosure to prevent temperature fluctuations that affect the solidification process. Which Material Provides Better Overall Tensile Strength, PLA or ABS? ABS is the material that provides better overall tensile strength. ABS has higher impact resistance and endures more stress before breaking or deforming. It is more flexible, allowing it to absorb forces without fracturing. PLA is more rigid and tends to break under stress, offering lower tensile strength. ABS is ideal for applications where durability and mechanical strength are required (automotive parts or functional components). PLA is more suited for decorative items that do not undergo significant mechanical stress. Which Material Shows Less Warping During Printing, PLA or ABS? PLA is the material that shows less warping during printing. PLA has a lower melting point and solidifies fast, which reduces the likelihood of warping as it cools. ABS tends to shrink more as it cools, leading to higher stress and warping on larger prints. PLA's lower temperature sensitivity makes it easier to print without the need for a heated bed or enclosure, unlike ABS, which requires both to prevent warping. It makes PLA a more reliable material for precise prints and smaller projects. Which Material Delivers Higher Dimensional Accuracy, PLA or ABS? PLA is the material that delivers higher dimensional accuracy. PLA has lower shrinkage during cooling, which results in fewer distortions and better precision in prints. ABS, on the other hand, tends to shrink more as it cools, leading to potential warping and dimensional inaccuracies. PLA's ease of printing without the need for a heated bed ensures that the printed object retains its intended shape and size. ABS requires more careful temperature control to maintain dimensional consistency, making PLA a more reliable material for accurate prints. Which Material Performs Better in Outdoor Environments, PLA or ABS? ABS is the material that performs better in outdoor environments. ABS has higher Ultraviolet (UV) resistance and withstands prolonged exposure to sunlight without degrading. PLA, being biodegradable, breaks down faster when exposed to outdoor elements (sunlight and moisture). ABS maintains its strength and color for a longer period, making it suitable for outdoor applications (automotive parts and garden tools). PLA’s sensitivity to environmental factors makes it more appropriate for indoor use or short-term outdoor projects. Which Material Has Superior Layer Adhesion, PLA or ABS? ABS is the material that has superior layer adhesion. ABS bonds better between layers due to its higher printing temperature and improved layer fusion. The higher extrusion temperature of ABS allows for better adhesion between layers, reducing the likelihood of delamination or layer separation. PLA, with its lower printing temperature, struggles to bond layers as effectively in prints that require strength and durability. ABS’s improved layer adhesion makes it ideal for functional parts that must endure stress and wear. Which Material Produces Stronger Functional Parts, PLA or ABS? ABS is the material that produces stronger functional parts. ABS has higher impact resistance and endures physical stress better than PLA, making it ideal for applications (automotive components or tools). PLA is more rigid but tends to be brittle, breaking under pressure or impact. ABS’s flexibility and durability allow it to withstand wear and tear, while PLA is more suited for decorative or low-stress applications. ABS’s ability to handle mechanical forces and higher temperatures makes it the preferred material for functional parts. Which Material Is More Resistant to Chemicals, PLA or ABS? ABS is a material that is more resistant to chemicals. ABS withstands exposure to a broader range of chemicals (oils, acids, and alkaline solutions) without degradation. PLA is more susceptible to chemical damage and likely breaks down when exposed to certain solvents, oils, or strong acids. For example, ABS is used in environments where chemical exposure is expected (plumbing or automotive parts). PLA’s lower resistance to chemicals limits its use in applications where durability against harsh substances is needed. Which Material Is More Flexible or Less Brittle, PLA or ABS? ABS is a material that is more flexible and less brittle. ABS has better impact resistance and bends without breaking, making it suitable for functional parts that need durability. PLA is more rigid and tends to be brittle, which makes it more likely to crack or break under stress. ABS’s flexibility allows it to absorb shocks and withstand mechanical forces better than PLA, making it more suitable for decorative or low-stress applications. ABS is the preferred choice due to its increased flexibility for parts exposed to regular handling or stress. Which Material Is Safer To Print Indoors, PLA or ABS? PLA is a material that is safer to print indoors. PLA emits fewer harmful fumes during printing, releasing biodegradable compounds (lactide). ABS releases more toxic fumes (styrene), which irritate the respiratory system and require proper ventilation. PLA is less likely to cause health concerns and is more suitable for indoor environments with limited airflow. ABS requires additional precautions (e.g., using an enclosure or ensuring good ventilation) when printing indoors due to its higher emission levels. What Are the Similarities Between PLA and ABS? The similarities between PLA and ABS are listed below. 3D Printing Compatibility : PLA and ABS are used for 3D printing. Each is compatible with consumer-grade 3D printers and is readily available in filament form. Ease of Use: Polylactic Acid and Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene are relatively simple to print with, though ABS requires a heated bed for optimal results. Its moderate printing temperatures make them accessible for general 3D printing applications. Strength and Durability : PLA and ABS offer adequate strength and durability for various printing needs. ABS is more flexible and durable, while PLA is more rigid but is suitable for a range of functional prints. Surface Finishing : PLA and ABS are post-processed to achieve smoother finishes. Sanding, painting, or chemical smoothing is possible with either material to improve the surface quality. What Are the Mutual Alternative 3D Filaments for PLA and ABS? The mutual alternative 3D filaments for PLA and ABS are listed below. Polyethylene Terephthalate Glycol (PETG): PETG is a versatile filament known for its durability, chemical resistance, and ease of use. The alternative combines the strength of ABS with the comfort of printing of PLA, making it a popular alternative. Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU): TPU is a flexible filament with excellent elasticity and abrasion resistance. It is ideal for creating rubber-like prints and is used for phone cases, wearables, and flexible parts. Nylon : Nylon is a strong, durable, and flexible filament that offers great impact resistance and wear properties. It is suitable for functional parts and mechanical applications, but it requires a heated bed to print correctly. Acrylonitrile Styrene Acrylate (ASA): For outdoor applications and parts exposed to the elements, printing ASA can be a strong alternative to ABS because it offers better UV resistance and outdoor durability. High Impact Polystyrene (HIPS): HIPS is used as a support material for ABS prints, but is printed on its own for low-stress applications. It is a good alternative when smooth surface finishes are needed and falls under the types of 3D filaments when considering its applications. events.before: Resources / 3D Printing Design / How to Smooth 3D Prints: PLA, ABS, and FDM Prints How to Smooth 3D Prints: PLA, ABS, and FDM Prints Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 26 min read Published May 24, 2023 Updated August 26, 2026 Your guide to smoothing options to get 3D printed parts with better aesthetics To smooth 3D prints, achieving a high-quality finish is essential for aesthetic appeal and functionality. A smooth surface increases visual appeal by minimizing visible layer lines and providing a more refined finish. The process makes the print more suitable for subsequent post-processing. Smoothing the surface promotes better adhesion for additional layers or paint, improving the print's durability and functionality. Proper surface preparation is essential to ensure optimal adhesion. Different filament types (such as PLA and ABS) and FDM-printed parts require specific smoothing techniques due to their varying material characteristics. Each filament behaves differently when exposed to heat, solvents, or abrasives. PLA prints can be smoothed using specific solvents such as ethyl acetate or through mechanical methods, while ABS prints are best smoothed with acetone vapor. FDM prints require a combination of sanding and chemical smoothing, depending on the material and finish desired. The guide details methods for how to smooth 3D prints, providing step-by-step instructions and practical tips for smoothing PLA prints, ABS prints, and other FDM prints. The guide ensures that novice and experienced users apply the correct methods. Various techniques (sanding, vapor smoothing, and chemical refinement) are discussed to help achieve a professional-quality finish. Each technique is tailored to the print material and desired results. Each method is explained in precise steps to ensure novice and experienced 3D printers learn how to make 3D prints smooth and improve their print quality through effective 3D print smoothing techniques. The 3D Prints that are smoothed using the proper methods are more appealing and suitable for further post-processing (painting, detailing, or functional use). 3D Print Smoothing Techniques 1. Using Paint and Sanding Material Using paint and sanding material is an effective method for smoothing 3D prints. A filler primer is applied first to fill minor gaps or imperfections, providing a more even surface once it dries. Sanding is used to smooth the surface. Sandpaper with varying grits is employed, starting with medium grit to address flaws and moving to finer grits for a polished finish. The technique helps achieve a smooth, professional appearance on 3D prints for materials (PLA or ABS). The process helps eliminate rough textures and uneven layers, which are common results of 3D printing. The method is beneficial when preparing the print for further painting or post-processing. 2. Using Abrasive Smoothing Methods Using abrasive smoothing methods is a common technique to refine the surface of 3D prints for materials (PLA, ABS, PETG, and nylon). The process involves using abrasive materials (sandpaper, grinding wheels, or abrasive pads) to remove rough spots and imperfections physically. The process starts with a medium grit to address larger imperfections, followed by progressively finer grits to achieve a smoother finish. Abrasive smoothing is done manually with sandpaper or with mechanical tools, depending on the print's size and desired finish. The method is effective for improving the appearance of 3D prints with visible layer lines or surface defects. The process provides control over the amount of smoothing, allowing for a customized finish. Abrasive smoothing is a cost-effective option that does not require specialized equipment, making it accessible for hobbyists and professionals. The primary advantage is its ability to achieve a smooth surface free from defects, improving the print's quality and preparing it for further post-processing (painting or coating). Cost : A few hundred dollars for the equipment, or you can have a service like Xometry do it. Try Xometry's Instant Quoting Engine® Test-drive a sample part to get instant pricing and DFM analysis Launch Demo "Currently Xometry only offers vapor smoothing for SLS and MJF nylon based materials, as the chemical solvent our network uses is compatible with nylons." Christian Tsu-Raun Team Lead, Manual Quoting 3. Finishing with Fine Sandpaper and Micro-Mesh Finishing with fine sandpaper and micro-mesh provides a detailed method for smoothing 3D prints when aiming for a high-quality finish. Fine sandpaper is used to smooth the print further after initial sanding with coarser grades, though it does not entirely remove all roughness. Progressing through medium to fine grits before using micro-mesh yields the best results. Micro-mesh pads are effective for refining the surface, working to smooth out micro-imperfections and providing a polished finish. The method is beneficial for smoothing out minor flaws and improving the appearance of the print. The process is effective for delicate projects or when a high-quality finish is essential. The use of micro-mesh and fine sandpaper offers a controlled, step-by-step approach to smoothing, allowing for greater precision than coarser methods. The result is a smooth surface that is ideal for subsequent painting or coating, or for displays where a polished finish is essential. 4. Using Polishing Compounds Using polishing compounds is an effective method for improving the surface finish of 3D prints to achieve a glossy, smooth appearance. Polishing compounds are applied to refine the surface further after the print has been sanded and most of the rough texture has been reduced. The compounds are designed to work with various materials (PLA and ABS) and contain fine abrasives that help minimize minor imperfections while providing a shiny finish. Polishing is done with a soft cloth or polishing tool, but proper technique is essential to ensure an even application and avoid overheating. Polishing compounds are beneficial for prints that require a glossy finish or improved appearance (display models). Achieving an appearance that mimics injection-molded plastic requires additional post-processing. The primary advantage of the method is its ability to reduce visible surface imperfections, improving the texture without causing damage when used correctly. Polishing compounds make 3D prints appear more polished and durable, ideal for final presentations or functional use where aesthetics are essential. 5. Automotive Filler Primer Automotive filler primer is an effective method for smoothing 3D prints when preparing them for painting or additional finishing. The product is designed to fill minor imperfections and layer lines that are common in 3D prints. The primer is applied as a thin coat over the surface, but multiple coats are needed to achieve a uniform texture. Primer is sanded carefully to smooth out the surface once the primer has dried, but excessive sanding disturbs the print's shape. The primer improves the appearance and increases the adhesion of subsequent paint layers, though its effectiveness in promoting adhesion depends on the print material and primer quality. The technique is beneficial for prints made of materials (ABS or PLA), where layer lines and surface irregularities are standard. Automotive filler primer is effective at creating a smoother base for painting, making it suitable for high-quality finishes. A primer's ability to fill imperfections and provide a better surface for painting makes it a helpful tool for achieving a professional, glossy appearance, but additional finishing steps are necessary for a flawless result. The method is beneficial when preparing prints for detailed painting or for situations where a smooth surface is essential. 6. Using Heat Gun Using a heat gun can reduce surface roughness on some 3D prints (including ABS), but it requires careful control to avoid warping. The heat gun works by applying controlled heat to the surface of the print, causing the plastic to soften. The softening allows the material to flow slightly, helping reduce minor imperfections (layer lines and rough spots). The process does not eliminate imperfections. The print is evenly heated by moving the heat gun over the surface, helping to achieve a more uniform finish. Careful control of the temperature and distance from the print is essential to avoid warping or distorting the model. The method is beneficial for prints with noticeable surface roughness or visible layer lines, though it is not as effective for deep imperfections. The heat gun helps smooth the print without extensive sanding, but light sanding is required to achieve the best finish. The process is beneficial for larger prints or models with complex geometries, where traditional sanding is difficult. The heat gun is cost-effective and easy to use, providing a more professional finish without the need for expensive or specialized equipment. 7. Chemical Smoothing (ABS) Chemical smoothing for ABS involves using solvents (acetone) to smooth the surface of 3D prints. The process works by exposing the print to acetone vapor, which softens the outer layer of the ABS material, allowing the surface to become smoother and more uniform. The process does not eliminate deeper imperfections (visible layer lines) while the softening provides a glossy finish. The print is placed in a sealed chamber with acetone, and the vapor gently softens the outer layers. The process helps smooth out the surface, but additional post-processing is necessary for a polished finish. The method is effective for improving the appearance of ABS prints when a smoother surface is desired. Achieving a high-gloss finish depends on the print's initial quality and the chemical smoothing process. Chemical smoothing reduces the visibility of layer lines, though its effectiveness varies based on print quality and acetone exposure time. The process is beneficial for functional or decorative items where a smoother finish is essential. The advantage of chemical smoothing is that it is able to smooth complex geometries without requiring extensive manual sanding, though fine control is needed in order not to over-smooth delicate areas. The process requires careful handling and proper ventilation, as acetone is a volatile chemical. The process is a cost-effective and efficient way to enhance ABS prints while requiring adequate safety precautions. 8. PLA Layer Vapor Smoothing PLA layer vapor smoothing is a technique used to improve the surface finish of PLA prints by applying a vapor of a solvent (ethyl acetate) to the print’s surface. The vapor gently softens the outer layer of the PLA material, causing it to flow and smooth out imperfections like visible layer lines and rough patches. The procedure does not ‘melt’ the material but softens it just enough to achieve a smoother finish. Solvent evaporates leaving behind a smoother and slightly glossy surface, which increases the appearance of the print. The level of shine varies depending on the solvent used and exposure time. The method requires careful control of vapor exposure to avoid over-softening the material, which leads to warping or excessive smoothing, affecting the print's shape. The technique is beneficial for PLA prints that require a smoother finish without extensive sanding or manual polishing. The processes reduce the need for further surface preparation but do not fully replace other post-processing steps. PLA layer vapor smoothing is effective for reducing the visibility of print lines and improving the surface finish. The degree of polish depends on solvent exposure and print quality. The process is relatively quick and efficient for prints with complex shapes where traditional sanding is time-consuming or complicated. The results are not always flawless, and additional polishing is necessary for a perfect finish. The Epoxy Resin Coating can be applied after vapor smoothing to provide a more refined, long-lasting finish for prints that require higher gloss or added durability. 9. Hot Water Smoothing (PLA) Hot water can soften PLA near its glass transition temperature, which may reduce minor surface imperfections but can also cause warping if not carefully controlled. The heat causes the PLA to become more pliable, allowing minor surface imperfections (layer lines and rough patches) to smooth out. The water temperature must be controlled to avoid melting the print, as water that is too hot causes deformation. The print is placed in hot water, around 60-70°C (140-158°F), and left for a brief period. The softened surface must then be smoothed manually or allowed to cool naturally, though some smoothing is required while the print is pliable. The method is helpful for PLA prints that require smoothing without solvents or abrasives. The process is cost-effective and straightforward, making it accessible for hobbyists and professionals. The effectiveness of the method depends on the size and complexity of the print. Hot water smoothing is effective for reducing the visibility of minor imperfections in prints that have not been exposed to solvents or chemicals. The technique is effective at repairing surface-level defects. The process requires careful attention to avoid overheating the print, as excessive heat causes warping or deformation. Hot water smoothing is ideal for smaller prints or areas with minor surface flaws, offering a quick and efficient way to increase the surface quality of PLA models, but larger prints or more significant imperfections require additional post-processing. "Smoothing 3D prints is less about chasing a perfectly glossy surface and more about understanding how each material responds to heat, solvents, and abrasion. When the post-processing method matches the filament’s behavior, surface quality improves predictably and without compromising part geometry." Audrius Zidonis PhD Principal Engineer at Zidonis Engineering 10. Cold Welding and Solvent Welding Solvent Welding (also called Cold welding) is primarily a bonding method for ABS prints that can also provide localized surface smoothing.Cold welding involves applying a solvent (acetone) directly to the surfaces of two parts to bond them together. The solvent softens the outer layers of the parts, allowing them to fuse at a molecular level, creating a smooth connection. The method is used to smooth the surface by softening imperfections and joining rough sections, though it does not eliminate all flaws. Solvent welding uses a similar process but focuses on applying the solvent to a single surface, softening it to reduce imperfections and layer lines. The process helps smooth the surface but does not fully address deep flaws. The methods are effective for improving the appearance and bonding strength of ABS prints when surface smoothing and part joining are needed. Cold welding is beneficial for joining parts, while solvent welding is ideal for refining the surface of a single print. Solvent welding is better suited for smoothing surfaces rather than joining multiple parts. The primary advantage of cold welding and solvent welding is their ability to create a smooth, unified surface or bond without the need for sanding or abrasive methods. The methods do not replace the need for polishing or finishing techniques for a flawless surface. Solvent welding works well for smoothing complex geometries and smaller prints, providing a quick and efficient way to refine the surface. Larger prints require additional methods to achieve a polished finish. The methods require careful handling of solvents and proper ventilation, as the solvents are flammable and harmful if inhaled. Always follow safety guidelines to minimize risks. 11. Using 3D Gloop Using 3D Gloop is an effective method for smoothing 3D prints made from PLA and ABS. 3D Gloop is a specialized smoothing solution designed to improve surface appearance by applying a thin layer to the print’s surface. The process softens the outer layer of the print and smooths out minor imperfections, giving it a smoother, glossier finish. The print is left to dry after application, resulting in a softer surface that reduces visible layer lines and imperfections. The primary advantage of 3D Gloop is its ease of use and convenience, as it does not require complex setups. The process requires careful application to avoid uneven layers. The method is beneficial for prints that need smoothing before painting, as it helps create a more uniform surface for better paint adhesion, although additional surface preparation is necessary. 3D Gloop is suited for PLA and ABS prints, providing a cost-effective solution to improve the finish of prints with minimal effort, though deeper imperfections are visible depending on the print's complexity. 12. Using XTC-3D Using XTC-3D is an effective method for smoothing 3D prints when aiming for a high-gloss, polished surface. XTC-3D is a two-part epoxy resin designed for smoothing and coating 3D printed objects. The resin helps fill in layer lines and minor imperfections when applied, resulting in a smoother, glossier finish. The process does not eliminate deep flaws or highly textured surfaces. The process involves mixing the two parts of the epoxy, applying it using a brush or spray, and allowing it to cure for the specified time. The result is a durable, smooth surface that improves the print's appearance and provides added protection, though proper application is essential to avoid streaks or uneven areas. The method is beneficial for prints that require a professional, polished look (display models or functional items) that need a refined finish. XTC-3D provides a durable coating that smooths the surface and adds protection to the print, though the level of durability depends on the print material and curing process. The process is effective for prints with visible layer lines or rough surfaces, filling in imperfections and creating a smoother finish. Deep flaws are visible. The main advantages of using XTC-3D Coating are its ability to smooth the surface, ease of application, and glossy finish. Achieving the best results depends on proper technique and curing time, making it a popular choice for 3D print post-processing. 13. Using Epoxy Resin Coating Using epoxy resin coating is an effective technique for smoothing and improving the surface of 3D prints for materials like PLA and ABS. The process involves applying a layer of epoxy resin over the print's surface, which helps fill in imperfections (layer lines and minor defects). The process does not eliminate deeper flaws or complex surface irregularities. The resin cures to form a smooth, glossy, and durable finish, though the final texture depends on application technique and curing conditions. Epoxy resin is applied using a brush, spray, or poured over the print, depending on the desired effect, print size, and complexity. The application method affects the finish, requiring more precision for specific geometries. The technique is beneficial for achieving a professional finish on 3D prints for items that are displayed or used in environments requiring durability and a refined appearance. Epoxy resin provides a hard, protective layer that improves the print's surface, making it more resistant to scratches, water, and wear. Formulation and application thickness determine the resistance thickness. The method provides the print with a polished, high-gloss look, making it suitable for functional or decorative objects. The degree of gloss depends on the resin type and curing conditions. The major advantage of using epoxy resin coating is its ability to create a smooth surface and improve surface durability. The final strength depends on the print material and the resin's properties. The results are worth the effort for projects requiring a high-quality finish, while the process is time-consuming. Patience is needed to ensure proper application and curing. 14. Using PolyMaker PolySmooth PVB Filament Using PolyMaker PolySmooth PVB filament is an effective method for smoothing 3D prints, for makers seeking a high-quality finish with minimal effort. PolySmooth is a specialized filament designed to be smoothed using isopropyl alcohol vapor. The outer layers soften when the printed object is exposed to isopropyl alcohol vapor, allowing imperfections such as layer lines to smooth out and giving the print a glossy, polished surface. The improved surface finish is essential for parts that undergo further processing (painting or functional applications), where surface smoothness impacts the final quality and performance. Frequently Asked Questions on How to Smooth 3D Prints What Is the Most Common Technique To Smoothen PLA 3D Prints? The most common techniques to smooth PLA 3D prints involve mechanical and coating-based post-processing rather than true vapor smoothing. PLA prints are typically smoothed using progressive sanding, fillers, primers, and surface coatings to reduce visible layer lines and improve surface finish. These methods refine the outer surface without melting the material, allowing for improved smoothness and controlled finishing. Excessive heat or aggressive processing can still cause warping or deformation, so careful control is required. Sanding is often performed in stages using increasingly fine grits, sometimes combined with filler primers or epoxy-based coatings to further reduce surface imperfections. The final appearance depends on surface preparation, material quality, and environmental factors such as temperature and humidity during finishing. These techniques help smooth surface imperfections but require careful control to avoid over-processing, which can affect the print’s shape or surface integrity. Even application is essential when sanding, applying fillers, primers, or coatings, as uneven treatment can lead to inconsistent texture or finish. Layer-by-layer surface refinement is important during sanding and filling to prevent over-sanding or localized surface damage. Abrasive tools like sandpaper remove rough patches, and solvents like acetone or isopropyl alcohol are used for surface refinement. Inconsistent application leads to streaks or patches that need touch-ups. Applying the solvent evenly and carefully controlling exposure time helps achieve a smooth, consistent finish. Overexposure to the solvent leads to deformation or uneven smoothing. What Is the Most Common Technique To Smoothen FDM 3D Prints? The most common technique to smooth FDM 3D prints is vapor smoothing, particularly for FDM materials that respond to solvents, such as ABS with acetone. The method helps reduce visible layer lines and create a smoother, glossier finish. The print is exposed to solvent vapor, which softens the surface without fully melting it, allowing the imperfections to become less noticeable. The technique reduces surface roughness but does not eliminate all flaws. Sanding, followed by chemical smoothing, is another method used. Sanding removes rough patches, and applying solvents (isopropyl alcohol or acetone) helps further refine the surface, filling in minor gaps and smoothing the texture. Excessive sanding or chemical exposure distorts the print. The best results are achieved by filling gaps and uneven areas during sanding before smoothing. Uneven sanding leads to inconsistent results. Even application of the solvent is essential to avoid uneven finishes, which lead to inconsistent gloss or texture. Control over the solvent application ensures a smoother, more consistent result. Careful attention to exposure time during vapor smoothing ensures the surface is smoothed effectively. Overexposure leads to distortion, and it's essential to monitor the process closely. The techniques improve the finish of FDM 3D prints , making them look more professional and polished. Post-processing (painting or detail finishing) is necessary for a flawless appearance, but it makes the prints suitable for further post-processing (painting). Why Are the 3D Printing Surfaces Not Smooth? The 3D printing surfaces are not smooth because of layer height, extrusion inconsistencies, cooling conditions, and filament quality. The layer height affects the surface finish. Higher layer heights result in more noticeable layer lines, making it harder to achieve a smooth 3D print. Lower layer heights produce a finer surface, but the process increases print time. Extrusion inconsistencies, caused by uneven filament feeding or temperature fluctuations in the hotend, lead to visible imperfections and gaps. The discrepancies were reduced by ensuring consistent filament flow and stabilizing the hotend temperature. Insufficient cooling with larger or intricate prints prevents proper solidification, leading to uneven surfaces. Proper cooling ensures more uniform solidification of each layer, improving surface quality. The quality of the filament plays a significant role. Low-quality filament contains impurities or has inconsistent diameters, resulting in rougher surfaces and poor print quality. Smoothing 3D prints improves the surface finish, but addressing underlying issues (layer height, extrusion consistency, and cooling conditions) is necessary to achieve a consistently smooth and high-quality print. Selecting the correct filler for the material is essential to ensure proper adhesion and smoothing. The filler helps fill remaining imperfections, such as small gaps or rough spots from the 3D printing process, though larger flaws require additional post-processing. The print is sanded down to create a smoother, more even surface after the filler has dried. Sanding must be done gradually, starting with coarser grits and moving to finer ones to avoid over-sanding. A coat of paint is applied to provide color and protection once the surface is refined. The effectiveness of the paint depends on the type of paint and surface preparation, including the application of a primer. The method is helpful for prints that need to be visually appealing or functional (display models, prototypes, or functional objects). The combination of filler and paint improves the finish by creating a smoother surface and adding durability. The durability depends on the type of filler and paint used. The main advantage of the method is its ability to improve the surface, transforming a rough 3D print into a smoother, glossier product. Achieving a high-quality finish requires careful application and curing. The technique is effective for prints requiring high-quality appearance, as the filler creates a clean base, and the paint provides the final touch for a polished finish. The longevity of the finish depends on the materials and environmental exposure. 17. 3D Pen Smoothing Tool The 3D pen smoothing tool is a specialized tool used to refine the surface of 3D prints by applying melted filament. The technique does not eliminate all surface defects, but it helps smooth out imperfections, especially larger ones. The pen works by heating the filament, which is extruded through the nozzle and applied directly onto the print's surface. The filament must be compatible with the print material for best results. Using the pen provides control over the smoothing process, allowing the pen to fill gaps, smooth layer lines, and repair minor defects. The method's effectiveness in large-scale smoothing or deeper defects is limited. The tool is used in a back-and-forth motion to blend the applied filament with the existing surface, but it must be used to avoid visible lines or uneven surfaces. The method is beneficial for minor surface corrections and fine details, for smaller prints or areas needing precise work. The process is not as effective for large-scale smoothing or major surface flaws. The primary advantage of using a 3D pen smoothing tool is its ability to directly control filament application and the smoothing process, although a steady hand is required to ensure uniformity. A versatile and accessible solution for addressing specific imperfections. The finish requires additional post-processing for a perfectly smooth finish, while it reduces the need for sanding. The result is a softer surface, though the level of polish varies depending on the technique used. The 3D pen smoothing tool is a valuable option for improving the appearance and quality of 3D prints, but additional steps are required for a fully polished look. What is the Purpose of Smoothing 3D Prints? The purpose of smoothing 3D prints is to improve the surface finish, reduce visible layer lines, and improve paint adhesion during post-processing. The process does not strengthen the part unless combined with additional treatments, and smoothing primarily improves surface finish rather than structural integrity. Smooth PLA prints create a more uniform surface that reduces rough textures and imperfections left by the 3D printing process. The smoother surface makes it easier to apply paint and coatings, as the smoother surface allows for better adhesion. Optimal paint adhesion requires priming. 3D print smoothing helps reduce layer lines, resulting in a more polished and professional look, though achieving a flawless finish requires further post-processing. Smoothing PLA prints or other 3D prints primarily improves aesthetics, with limited impact on mechanical performance. The direct effect on structural integrity is limited without reinforcing methods or materials. The improved surface finish is essential for parts that undergo further processing (painting or functional applications), where surface smoothness impacts the final quality and performance. Frequently Asked Questions on How to Smooth 3D Prints What Is the Most Common Technique To Smoothen PLA 3D Prints? The most common techniques to smooth PLA 3D prints involve mechanical and coating-based post-processing rather than true vapor smoothing. PLA prints are typically smoothed using progressive sanding, fillers, primers, and surface coatings to reduce visible layer lines and improve surface finish. These methods refine the outer surface without melting the material, allowing for improved smoothness and controlled finishing. Excessive heat or aggressive processing can still cause warping or deformation, so careful control is required. Sanding is often performed in stages using increasingly fine grits, sometimes combined with filler primers or epoxy-based coatings to further reduce surface imperfections. The final appearance depends on surface preparation, material quality, and environmental factors such as temperature and humidity during finishing. Chemical solvents like isopropyl alcohol or acetone are generally not effective for smoothing standard PLA and are used only with specific PLA-compatible materials or coatings. These techniques help smooth surface imperfections but require careful control to avoid over-processing, which can affect the print’s shape or surface integrity. Even application is essential when sanding, applying fillers, primers, or coatings, as uneven treatment can lead to inconsistent texture or finish. Uneven sanding or coating often requires additional touch-ups to restore uniformity. Layer-by-layer surface refinement is important during sanding and filling to prevent over-sanding or localized surface damage. When applied correctly, these methods are effective for achieving smoother PLA 3D prints , making the final product more visually appealing and suitable for further post-processing such as painting or detailing. These approaches provide reliable solutions for improving PLA print surface quality while maintaining dimensional control. What Is the Most Common Technique To Smoothen ABS 3D Prints? The most common technique to smoothen ABS 3D Prints is vapor smoothing, which uses acetone vapor to soften the surface and reduce layer lines. The process does not eliminate deep imperfections, but it helps improve the finish. The acetone vapor softens the outer layer, allowing it to smooth out, but it does not fully melt the material. The process creates a smoother, glossy finish, though the degree of gloss depends on exposure time. Abrasive tools like sandpaper remove rough patches, and solvents like acetone or isopropyl alcohol are used for surface refinement. The combination helps further smooth the surface but requires multiple passes. Smoothing ABS 3D Prints requires an even coating and consistent layer filling to prevent uneven gloss and texture. Inconsistent application leads to streaks or patches that need touch-ups. Applying the solvent evenly and carefully controlling exposure time helps achieve a smooth, consistent finish. Overexposure to the solvent leads to deformation or uneven smoothing. What Is the Most Common Technique To Smoothen FDM 3D Prints? The most common technique to smooth FDM 3D prints is vapor smoothing, particularly for FDM materials that respond to solvents, such as ABS with acetone. The method helps reduce visible layer lines and create a smoother, glossier finish. The print is exposed to solvent vapor, which softens the surface without fully melting it, allowing the imperfections to become less noticeable. The technique reduces surface roughness but does not eliminate all flaws. Sanding, followed by chemical smoothing, is another method used. Sanding removes rough patches, and applying solvents (isopropyl alcohol or acetone) helps further refine the surface, filling in minor gaps and smoothing the texture. Excessive sanding or chemical exposure distorts the print. The best results are achieved by filling gaps and uneven areas during sanding before smoothing. Uneven sanding leads to inconsistent results. Even application of the solvent is essential to avoid uneven finishes, which lead to inconsistent gloss or texture. Control over the solvent application ensures a smoother, more consistent result. Careful attention to exposure time during vapor smoothing ensures the surface is smoothed effectively. Overexposure leads to distortion, and it's essential to monitor the process closely. The techniques improve the finish of FDM 3D prints , making them look more professional and polished. Post-processing (painting or detail finishing) is necessary for a flawless appearance, but it makes the prints suitable for further post-processing (painting). Why Are the 3D Printing Surfaces Not Smooth? The 3D printing surfaces are not smooth because of layer height, extrusion inconsistencies, cooling conditions, and filament quality. The layer height affects the surface finish. Higher layer heights result in more noticeable layer lines, making it harder to achieve a smooth 3D print. Lower layer heights produce a finer surface, but the process increases print time. Extrusion inconsistencies, caused by uneven filament feeding or temperature fluctuations in the hotend, lead to visible imperfections and gaps. The discrepancies were reduced by ensuring consistent filament flow and stabilizing the hotend temperature. Insufficient cooling with larger or intricate prints prevents proper solidification, leading to uneven surfaces. Proper cooling ensures more uniform solidification of each layer, improving surface quality. The quality of the filament plays a significant role. Low-quality filament contains impurities or has inconsistent diameters, resulting in rougher surfaces and poor print quality. Smoothing 3D prints improves the surface finish, but addressing underlying issues (layer height, extrusion consistency, and cooling conditions) is necessary to achieve a consistently smooth and high-quality print. events.before: Resources / 3D Printing Design / TPE vs. TPU: Differences and Comparison TPE vs. TPU: Differences and Comparison Written by Dean McClements 8 min read Published August 15, 2022 Updated September 3, 2026 Learn about the advantages, disadvantages, and properties of these 3D printing materials. TPE (Thermoplastic Elastomer) is a rubber that has both thermoplastic and elastomer properties. TPU (Thermoplastic Polyurethane), on the other hand, is a form of TPE. TPU and TPE are flexible filaments used as 3D printing materials for designs that require stretch or bend qualities. They also give a “soft-to-the-touch” quality to printed products. In general, TPEs tend to be softer and more flexible compared to TPUs. Because TPU is still flexible but more rigid, it is also an easier material with which to print. However, TPE is more commonplace because it has been on the market for a longer time. TPE is also generally less expensive compared to TPU. TPU performs well in heavier, tougher, and more durable prototypes, whereas TPE filament is more geared for lighter, softer, and more flexible models. In this article, we are going to look at TPE vs. TPU in terms of their differences, their applications, and the properties that make them unique in the additive manufacturing industry. TPE Definition and Comparison to TPU TPE is known for its robustness and flexibility. It is available as filament for FDM printers and as a powder for SLS machines. Though TPE is still fairly new to the additive manufacturing industry, it has been around as a material for industrial use since the 1950s. EOS was the first company to launch TPE as a material for SLS printing back in 2013. TPE goes by the name PrimePart ST (PEBA 2301). This introduction was followed by the launch of CRP Technology’s TPE material, called Windform® RL. As a polymer material, TPE combines the characteristics of thermoplastic and thermoset vulcanized rubber. Variants of TPE include a range of flexible materials, such as Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU), Thermoplastic Polyamide (TPA), and Thermoplastic Copolyester (TPC). TPE printed models and prototypes have been used in industries such as automotive and medical. TPE has been used in the manufacturing of sports shoes and can also be found in electronics—for example, the plastic casing around some headphone cables or any other application where rubber-like qualities are required. Advantages of TPE Compared to TPU TPE has the following advantages when compared to TPU: TPE has been on the market for longer and is, therefore, more common. TPE is softer and more flexible compared to TPU. TPE can be used as a flexible stabilizer. It is not only used to print an entire model but can be used to print an intermediate layer. TPE is generally cheaper compared to TPU. Some TPEs can be more readily recycled than TPUs. Disadvantages of TPE Compared to TPU TPE has the following disadvantages compared to TPU: TPE is not beginner-friendly. Printer settings have to be very precise in order to achieve the desired results. After printing, you have to rework almost every model printed with TPE. TPE is more temperature sensitive compared to other elastomers, such as TPU. TPU Definition and Comparison to TPE TPU and TPE form part of the same family. BF Goodrich (now known as Lubrizol Advanced Materials) invented TPU in 1959; it is not a recently discovered material. However, its application in 3D printing is still relatively new. Due to its unique properties, TPU has been gaining interest in the additive manufacturing industry. Its printed products have been applied to various industries. TPU can be used as printing material in two types of 3D printers—Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) printers and Selective Laser Sintering (SLS) printers. With FDM printers, the material in filament form is used to print the desired models. With SLS, a powder form is used. In the long run, printing with an FDM printer will be more cost-effective. TPU comes in a wide range of opaque colors as well as transparent. Its surface finish can range from smooth to rough (to provide grip). One of the unique features of TPU is that its hardness can be customized. This ability to control hardness can result in materials ranging from soft (rubbery) to hard (rigid plastic). The application of TPU is very versatile. Industries that use TPU printed products include aerospace, automotive, footwear, sports, and medical. TPU is also used as a casing for wires in the electrical industry and as protective cases for electronic devices, such as mobile phones or tablets. Try Xometry's Instant Quoting Engine® Test-drive a sample part to get instant pricing and DFM analysis Launch Demo Strain relief made in TPU, printed and vapor-smoothed by Xometry. Advantages of TPU Compared to TPE When comparing TPE vs. TPU, TPU has the following advantages over TPE: TPU is more abrasion resistant than TPE. This property makes TPU last longer in working parts. TPU retains its elastic properties in colder temperatures. TPU naturally has a higher resistance to chemicals, such as oils, greases, and a variety of solvents. TPU has a smooth finish, while TPE has a rubbery texture. TPU is less prone to shrinking compared to TPE. Disadvantages of TPU Compared to TPE TPU has the following disadvantages when compared to TPE: TPU can be difficult to post-process due to its abrasion and chemical resistance. TPU is hygroscopic in nature. This means it absorbs moisture from air humidity. Comparison Table Between TPE and TPU The table below shows a comparison between TPE and TPU: Table 1. TPE vs. TPU Comparison Attribute TPE TPU Attribute Extruder temperature TPE 210–260 °C (varies) TPU 220–250 °C (varies) Attribute Bed temperature TPE Up to 110 °C (varies) TPU Up to 60 °C (varies) Attribute Impact resistant TPE Yes TPU Yes Attribute Waterproof TPE Yes TPU Yes Attribute UV resistant TPE Yes TPU Yes Attribute Chemical resistance TPE Med TPU Med-High Attribute Abrasion resistance TPE Med-Low TPU High Attribute Heat resistance TPE High TPU High Attribute Strength TPE Low TPU Med-High Attribute Flexibility TPE High TPU Med-High Attribute Recommended printing speed TPE 5–50+ mm/s (varies) TPU 5–50+ mm/s (varies) Attribute Cost (per kg) TPE $40+ TPU $45+ Though TPE and TPU do differ, they also have some overlapping qualities. Both TPE and TPU are waterproof, UV resistant, and have good heat and impact resistance. TPE vs. TPU: Applications Comparison TPE is ideal for applications where flexible models are required, including 3D printed rubber parts such as sports gear grips (e.g., hockey stick handles), toys, mouthpieces in the medical industry, waterproof seals, airbag covers, and bumpers. TPU, on the other hand, offers a combination of scratch and abrasion resistance. This material is used in producing console parts, instrument panels, athletic shoes, and seals & gaskets. TPE vs. TPU: Part Accuracy Comparison Because TPE is more prone to shrinkage compared to TPU, it is also more difficult to print dimensionally accurate models with TPE. TPU is more rigid and easier with which to print and generally yields more accurate print results. TPE vs. TPU: Speed Comparison The speed setting for both print materials depends on the desired properties, for example, the flexibility of the end product. Appropriate print settings will depend on the type of TPE and TPU used, the manufacturer and model of the printer, and the set layer thickness. The required printing speed of TPE and TPU are in a similar range, 5–50 mm/s. In rare cases, both TPE and TPU can print at higher speeds. However, for accurate results, it is recommended to use printing speeds below 35 mm/s. TPE vs. TPU: Surface Comparison TPU tends to have a smoother surface finish compared to TPE, which usually has a rubber-like finish. TPE vs. TPU: Heat Resistance Comparison Both TPE and TPU filaments offer good heat resistance. TPE vs. TPU: Biodegradability Comparison Both TPU and TPE biodegrade in 3–5 years and are therefore considered eco-friendly 3D printing materials. TPE vs. TPU: Toxicity Comparison Although TPU is non-toxic in nature, it releases harmful fumes when exposed to fire or other chemicals. When burnt, TPU gives off a distinct odor that can cause headaches whereas TPE is non-toxic and has a faint aroma when burnt. TPE vs. TPU: Cost Comparison The relative costs of TPE vs. TPU per kg vary across the different brands. Popular brands of TPE filament, such as eSun TPE, Matterhackers, and 3dXFlex TPE range from $40/kg up to ~$140/kg. Some popular brands of TPU filament include Kodak Flex TPU (~$65/kg), Ultimaker TPU (~$90/kg), MatterHackers TPU (~$45–$55/kg), Polymaker PolyFlex (~$50–90/kg), and NinjaTek (~$110–$180/kg), among others. The following material is considered a mutual alternative to TPE and TPU: TPC (Thermoplastic Copolyester): TPC, just like TPE and TPU, is a rubber-like filament used in the 3D printing industry. It also boasts high-temperature resistance, good chemical resistance, high strength, and excellent UV resistance. Similarities Between TPE and TPU TPE and TPU share the following similarities: TPU and TPE are both thermoplastic elastomers that offer stretch and bend qualities in a print. Both TPE and TPU offer excellent colorability and clarity. TPE and TPU have similar printing speeds. events.before: Resources / Blog / Congratulations to our 2019 Engineering Student of the Year Congratulations to our 2019 Engineering Student of the Year Written by Serena Ngoh 5 min read Published October 9, 2020 Updated August 21, 2026 We’re awarding UT Austin graduate and future Berkeley PhD candidate Daniel Teal for his astounding commitment to engineering excellence. Gaithersburg, MD, June 2019 -- We’d like to congratulate recent graduate Daniel Teal for winning the 2019 Xometry Engineering Student of the Year Competition. We had dozens of qualified nominees, but Daniel stood out from our very strong pool of candidates by demonstrating incredible academic excellence, creativity, and a passion for engineering in his four years at the University of Texas at Austin. Teal graduated this past May with dual degrees in Mechanical Engineering and Mathematics with a specialization in scientific computation. He was nominated by Dr. Scott Evans, Director of Texas Inventionworks, the engineering makerspace and manufacturing program, and a lecturer at the School of Integrated Design. I sat down with Teal to discuss his past four years at UT Austin, as well his future plans as a professional engineer. What was your first significant engineering project in college? In high school, I was in my school’s FIRST robotics club, so when I came to UT I wanted to keep building robots. I joined the UT Robotics and Automation Society in the fall of 2015 and won their annual Robotathon with an autonomous Roomba that moved ping pong balls and marbles around. Try Xometry's Instant Quoting Engine® Test-drive a sample part to get instant pricing and DFM analysis Launch Demo The balancing robot Teal created under Evans’s mentorship. The autonomous Roomba that Teal built to compete in Robotathon 2015. The balancing robot Teal created under Evans’s mentorship. The autonomous Roomba that Teal built to compete in Robotathon 2015. 1 2 In the spring, I built a balancing robot that was supposed to climb stairs. It rolled and moved around just fine, but it couldn’t climb stairs. [laughs] When I was assembling it [in the school’s makerspace], Scott walked by at the very moment I plugged in a wire into the wrong spot and caused some electrical components to go up in smoke. That was the beginning of a close mentorship. In your nomination, Professor Evans mentioned your various leadership and community roles at UT Austin. Can you speak to these roles more? I worked at the makerspace, now called Texas Inventionworks , all my four years. I helped train students both in how to use the machines and how to design parts specifically for the makerspace machines, helped keep things organized and standardized, and made sure all the machines were running. Last fall of 2018, I stepped up from my webmaster role in the Robotics and Automation Society to lead the organization of the Robotathon. The goal of the competition is to teach about 100 engineering freshman how to build a simple robot. Teams of freshmen are paired with upperclassmen, who conduct workshops on everything from programming a microcontroller to CAD design to producing the hardware in the makerspace. The final robots competed in a classic sumo robot fighting competition to push each other out of the arena. Can you tell us about your organization of the UT Austin’s first Create-a-thon? As part of the Mechanical Engineering Undergraduate Advisory Board, which serves primarily to improve the mechanical engineering curriculum at UT Austin, I proposed and helped run our first (and later, second) annual Create-a-thon, a hardware hackathon, because I wanted people to experience an event like a software hackathon but with physical stuff. I wanted people to have the chance to build whatever they wanted. That’s usually hard because it requires expensive materials and tools. Once we secured funding for requested materials and room in the makerspace, we gave teams of students 24 hours to build and present their creations. The first year, the final projects included a robot that drew art based off of brainwaves and an automated discada maker. That’s a kind of Mexican food. There was also a motion-activated turtle lamp—it was whimsical, but it worked well and even won an award from our entrepreneurial engineering program here on campus. Pictured above: The attendees of the first Create-a-thon at UT Austin. Teal poses in the front row on the far right What are some other hardware projects you’re proud of? I built a jumping robot once, and then a six-legged walking robot, which was cool because it had multiple motors and many moving pieces. This past year, some classmates and I motorized a couch. We put wheels, motors, and a Raspberry Pi computer on a couch from the robotics club office and controlled it with a gamepad. The couch runs Linux—that’s something you don’t hear very often. A first prototype of the hexapod robot. The motorized couch traveling across the UT Austin campus. A first prototype of the hexapod robot. 1 2 What are your future plans now that you’ve graduated? In the fall I’m heading to a Ph.D. program at [The University of California,] Berkeley to research advanced manufacturing in nanotechnology. This will be building upon my research under various professors here at UT Austin and my summer research programs at Cornell and [the National Institute of Materials Science] in Tsubuka, Japan. I’ll be attempting to build tiny robots—smaller than a human hair—but will focus on improving or creating new manufacturing techniques to make them. Any advance in nanotechnology manufacturing is important because it can potentially be used to build better solar cells, water desalination filters, and batteries. My goal is to discover how to use these techniques to make things with more small-scale detail to make all machines better. How will you apply your nanotechnology research? I have ideas, but I don’t know for sure. You could use this nanotechnology to create a chemical sensor for microfluidics, or you could use nanowires to push cells around for microbiology research. But you don’t necessarily know what something will be useful for—you can’t be absolutely certain until you’ve made it work. I’ve learned that’s how half of all engineering works.
