Hygienic Properties: Stainless steel advantages feature a smooth, non-porous surface that prevents bacterial buildup, making it ideal for environments that require high sanitation standards in medical and food-handling settings. Recyclability : Stainless steel is 100% recyclable, conserving resources and reducing waste during manufacturing and end-of-life processes. What are the Disadvantages of Stainless Steel? The disadvantages of Stainless Steel are listed below. High Cost: Stainless steel production involves expensive alloying elements (chromium, nickel, and molybdenum), which increase its cost compared to materials (carbon steel or aluminum). Pitting Corrosion: Stainless steel is susceptible to localized corrosion in chloride-rich environments, where pitting occurs due to the breakdown of the protective chromium oxide layer. Difficult Machinability: Stainless steel presents challenges in machining and forming due to its hardness and work-hardening characteristics, requiring specialized tools and slower cutting speeds. Poor Thermal Conductivity: Stainless steel has lower thermal conductivity compared to metals (copper or aluminum), making it less efficient for heat transfer applications. Heavy Weight: Stainless steel has a higher density than materials, including aluminum, which increases weight and limits its use where lightweight construction is required. Expansion Under Heat: Stainless steel exhibits greater thermal expansion than some alternative metals, which causes dimensional changes in high-temperature applications. Surface Contamination Risk: Improper fabrication or cleaning leads to surface contamination, reducing corrosion resistance and appearance quality. What are the Properties of Stainless Steel? The properties of Stainless Steel are listed below. Corrosion Resistance : Stainless steel resists rust and oxidation through a passive chromium oxide film that shields the surface from environmental exposure. Austenitic grades such as 304 and 316 offer excellent corrosion resistance, with 316 containing molybdenum that improves performance in chloride environments, while ferritic grades provide good resistance in less aggressive conditions. Martensitic grades have moderate corrosion resistance but gain higher strength through heat treatment for mechanical applications. High Tensile Strength : Stainless steel exhibits excellent tensile strength and load-bearing capacity. Austenitic grades combine moderate to high strength with superior ductility, ferritic grades provide good strength and dimensional stability, and martensitic steels achieve the highest strength after quenching and tempering. Thermal Conductivity : Stainless steel has lower thermal conductivity than carbon steel, but provides consistent heat distribution in industrial equipment. Ferritic types conduct heat more efficiently than austenitic grades, making them suitable for exhaust systems and heat exchangers. Hardness : Martensitic stainless steels achieve high hardness through heat treatment, ferritic types offer moderate hardness, and austenitic steels have lower hardness but good formability. Ductility and Formability : Stainless steel retains ductility under stress, allowing fabrication into complex shapes. Austenitic grades exhibit the best formability due to their face-centered cubic structure, ferritic steels provide moderate flexibility, and martensitic types are less ductile after heat treatment. Magnetic and Non-Magnetic Behavior : Ferritic and martensitic steels are magnetic because of their body-centered cubic structure, while austenitic steels are non-magnetic in the annealed condition but become slightly magnetic after cold working. Thermal Expansion : Stainless steel expands when heated, with austenitic types showing the highest thermal expansion, while ferritic and martensitic steels exhibit lower rates. Reinforcement Bars: Stainless steel is used in reinforcement bars to strengthen concrete structures exposed to moisture, chlorides, or acidic conditions. Stainless steel corrosion resistance extends the service life of bridges, tunnels, and coastal buildings where environmental stress is high. Cladding and Facades: Stainless steel is used in exterior cladding and architectural facades for its durability, corrosion resistance, and visual appeal. Stainless steel maintains structural integrity under temperature fluctuations and increases building aesthetics through reflective or textured finishes. Structural Beams and Columns: Stainless steel is used in beams, columns, and load-bearing frameworks in large buildings and industrial facilities. Stainless steel has high tensile strength and resistance to deformation, supporting stability in areas exposed to vibration, heat, and heavy loads. Handrails and Balustrades: Stainless steel is used in handrails, balustrades, and staircases because it resists wear, provides safety, and maintains an attractive appearance in indoor and outdoor environments. Roofing and Drainage Systems: Stainless steel is used in roofing panels, gutters, and downpipes for its ability to resist corrosion and withstand extreme weather conditions while maintaining performance over extended service periods. Fasteners and Connectors: Stainless steel is used in bolts, screws, and brackets that secure structural components. Its corrosion resistance ensures reliability in humid, marine, and industrial environments. Expansion Joints and Fittings : Stainless steel is used in construction fittings and expansion joints where corrosion resistance and fatigue strength are required to handle movement, pressure, and temperature variations. Bridges and Monuments: Stainless steel is used in bridge components, railings, and monuments where exposure to rain, salt, and pollutants demands long-term durability and low maintenance. What Role does Stainless Steel Play in Automotive Safety Features? Stainless steel plays a valuable role in automotive safety by providing strength, durability, and corrosion resistance in components exposed to harsh conditions. Stainless steel is used in exhaust systems, fasteners, trim, and select reinforcement zones where resistance to heat, moisture, and corrosive gases is critical. Exhaust systems are stable and provide long-term performance due to stainless steel's ability to withstand high temperatures and corrosive emissions. Stainless steel contributes durability and corrosion resistance in selected automotive components exposed to heat and environmental stress, while crash-energy absorption relies primarily on high-strength carbon steels or aluminum alloys. Stainless steel improves specific components where mechanical strength and environmental resistance are essential for safe and reliable vehicle operation, while most vehicle crash structures rely on high-strength carbon steel or aluminum alloys for impact protection. What Are the Benefits of Stainless Steel in Food Packaging? The benefits of stainless steel in food packaging are evident in its hygienic, corrosion-resistant, and non-reactive qualities that protect food integrity during processing, storage, and transport. Stainless steel's smooth, non-porous surface prevents bacterial growth and allows effective cleaning and sterilization, ensuring compliance with strict hygiene standards. The corrosion resistance of stainless steel maintains structural durability when exposed to moisture, salts, and acidic foods, preventing contamination and material degradation. The stainless steel non-reactive nature ensures that no chemical interaction occurs between the packaging and food, preserving flavor, color, and nutritional value. The material’s strength and impact resistance make it suitable for reusable containers, processing tanks, and handling systems, supporting efficiency across industrial operations. The combination of cleanliness, chemical stability, and durability establishes stainless steel as a preferred material for food packaging and storage applications worldwide. What is the Cost of Stainless Steel Compared to Other Metals? The cost of stainless steel compared to other metals ranges from [$ 2,000 to $3,500] per metric ton, higher than carbon steel at $600- to $1,000 and aluminum at [$1,500–2,400]. Carbon steel costs around [$600 to $ 1,000] per metric ton, while aluminum ranges from [$ 1,500 to $2,400] per ton, subject to fluctuations in supply and demand. The higher cost of stainless steel results from the presence of alloying elements (chromium, nickel, and molybdenum), along with energy-intensive refining processes required to achieve corrosion resistance and mechanical strength. Stainless steel delivers long-term economic advantages in applications where durability, hygiene, and minimal maintenance are essential despite the elevated initial expense. Stainless steel's resistance to rust, chemical exposure, and surface wear extends the lifespan of structures, machinery, and medical devices, offsetting the higher upfront cost in environments demanding longevity and reliability. How is Stainless Steel Recycled? Stainless steel is recycled by collecting scrap material from manufacturing plants, construction sites, and consumer products, then processing it through a series of controlled metallurgical stages to recover its full properties. The process begins with sorting the scrap based on magnetic response and approximate composition to ensure consistency in alloy content. The sorted stainless steel is melted in an electric arc furnace, where impurities are removed and alloying elements (chromium, nickel, and molybdenum) are balanced to achieve the desired grade. Refinement through Argon Oxygen Decarburization (AOD) or vacuum treatment ensures precise chemical composition and purity. The molten stainless steel is cast into slabs, billets, or ingots that are later rolled and shaped into new products once refined. The recycling process reduces the need for raw material extraction, minimizes energy use, and supports sustainable manufacturing by maintaining material quality across multiple life cycles. The ability of stainless steel to retain its original strength, corrosion resistance, and durability makes it one of the most sustainable materials in industrial and structural applications. Is Stainless Steel Easier to Mold than Aluminum? No, Aluminum is easier to mold than stainless steel because of its lower melting point, softer texture, and higher malleability, which allow it to form complex shapes under less pressure and lower temperatures. Aluminum melts at 660 degrees Celsius, while stainless steel melts between 1,400 and 1,530 degrees Celsius, making stainless steel more challenging to mold and shape. The softer nature of aluminum enables efficient casting, extrusion, and stamping processes that reduce tooling wear and energy requirements. Stainless steel requires higher forming forces, specialized equipment, and precise temperature control due to its hardness and strength. Stainless steel provides superior durability, corrosion resistance, and wear protection despite being more difficult to mold, making it ideal for applications requiring long-term performance and structural integrity. The Aluminum remains the preferred material for molding processes that prioritize ease of shaping, lower energy use, and lightweight production. Does Stainless Steel Have Higher Abrasion Resistance than Carbon Steel? Yes, martensitic stainless steels can have higher abrasion resistance than many carbon steels due to their high hardness after heat treatment. Martensitic stainless steels, which are high in carbon and are heat-treated, exhibit excellent hardness and wear resistance, making them suitable for components exposed to friction and mechanical wear. Chromium and molybdenum in stainless steel improve corrosion and pitting resistance, which helps maintain surface integrity under abrasive conditions. Austenitic stainless steels (304 or 316) are softer and have lower abrasion resistance than hardened carbon steel . The superior combination of hardness, corrosion resistance, and surface durability in martensitic stainless steels gives them an advantage in high-abrasion environments. Is Stainless Steel More Impact-Resistant than Cast Iron? Yes, stainless steel is more impact-resistant than cast iron. Stainless steel combines strength, ductility, and toughness, allowing it to absorb energy and deform under stress rather than fracture. Gray cast iron is hard but brittle due to its graphite flake structure, which creates points of weakness. Gray cast iron is prone to cracking or shattering under sudden impact or heavy loads. Stainless steel maintains structural integrity under fluctuating mechanical stresses, making it suitable for construction, automotive components, and pressure vessels. The combination of toughness and resistance to brittle failure gives stainless steel a clear advantage in impact-resistant performance over gray cast iron. Does Stainless Steel Have Superior Thermal Insulation Properties Compared to Copper? No, stainless steel does not have superior thermal insulation properties compared to copper. Copper possesses higher thermal conductivity, averaging around 400 watts per meter-kelvin, while stainless steel averages between 14 and 20 watts per meter-kelvin. The high conductivity of copper allows it to transfer heat efficiently, making it the preferred material in applications (heat exchangers, wiring, and cookware). Stainless steel is a poor conductor of heat but is valued for its strength, corrosion resistance, and ability to maintain performance in harsh or corrosive environments. The material's lower thermal conductivity helps in situations where controlled or gradual heat transfer is required (in industrial processing equipment and specific food applications). Stainless steel offers mechanical durability and chemical stability that make it suitable for structural and hygienic applications where heat resistance and longevity are essential, while copper remains superior for efficient heat transfer. Is Stainless Steel More Biodegradable than Cobalt-Chromium (Co-Cr)? No, stainless steel nor cobalt-chromium (Co-Cr) is biodegradable. Stainless steel and cobalt-chromium are corrosion-resistant and designed for long-term stability, but cobalt-chromium exhibits superior wear resistance and biocompatibility, making it more suitable for permanent medical implants. Stainless steel 316L is used for temporary implants and surgical tools. Stainless steel is fully recyclable, while not biodegradable, allowing efficient recovery and reuse. The Cobalt-Chromium remains the preferred choice in orthopedic and dental applications requiring durability and minimal biological reactivity, whereas stainless steel provides cost-effective performance for short-term medical and structural uses. Does Stainless Steel Perform Better in Low-Temperature Environments than Brass? Yes, austenitic stainless steels (grades 304 and 316) perform better in low-temperature environments than brass because their properties retain strength, toughness, and ductility even under cryogenic conditions. Brass loses ductility and becomes brittle in extreme cold, increasing the risk of cracking under stress. The crystal structure of austenitic stainless steel allows it to absorb impact and mechanical loads without fracture, making it suitable for cryogenic storage tanks, pipelines, and components used in refrigeration and aerospace systems. The material's corrosion resistance further increases performance in low-temperature, moisture-prone environments. The Brass remains useful for moderate temperature applications, but austenitic stainless steel offers superior reliability and mechanical stability under severe cold conditions. Is Stainless Steel More Easily Recycled than 6061 Aluminum Alloy? Yes, stainless steel can be considered easier to recycle than 6061 aluminum alloy, depending on the criteria used. Stainless steel tolerates mixed scrap streams, can be remelted repeatedly without significant loss of mechanical or chemical properties, and is efficiently recovered in large-scale recycling systems. The 6061 aluminum alloy is also highly recyclable, but requires more precise grade separation to maintain its strength and corrosion resistance. Stainless steel’s tolerance for mixed scrap and its stable properties after remelting often make it favorable in heavy industrial recycling environments. Does Stainless Steel Offer More Structural Stability than Titanium in High-Performance Settings? No, stainless steel does not offer more structural stability than titanium in high-performance settings. Titanium has a superior strength-to-weight ratio, maintaining structural integrity under extreme mechanical stress while being lighter than stainless steel (4.5 g/cm³ vs 7.8 g/cm³). Titanium is ideal for aerospace, military, and high-speed automotive applications where weight reduction is critical for performance and efficiency. Stainless steel provides excellent strength, toughness, and corrosion resistance, and even outperforms titanium at very high temperatures in some cases, but its higher density limits its suitability for weight-sensitive designs. Titanium’s combination of high tensile strength, fatigue resistance, and thermal stability gives it a clear advantage in advanced engineering applications requiring performance and lightweight construction. Is Stainless Steel More Resistant to Fatigue than 7075 Aluminum Alloy ? Some stainless steel grades, such as martensitic and precipitation-hardening types, have higher fatigue resistance than 7075 aluminum alloy. Stainless steel’s toughness, dense microstructure, and alloying elements (chromium and nickel) allow it to resist crack initiation and propagation under repeated cyclic loading. Aluminum alloy 7075 is firm and lightweight, but is susceptible to corrosion and surface defects, which reduce its fatigue life. Stainless steel is therefore preferred for components subjected to repeated stress and vibration fasteners, springs, and rotating machinery), where long-term durability under mechanical strain is critical. A stainless steel combination of fatigue resistance, toughness, and corrosion resistance enables superior performance over 7075 Aluminum Alloy in demanding service conditions. Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 22 min read Published December 4, 2025 Updated August 26, 2026 Viscosity is the measure of a fluid’s resistance to flow. Viscosity definition indicates how thick or thin a fluid is and determines how easily it flows under an applied force. A fluid with high viscosity<dynamic-value> honey, flows slowly, while a fluid with low viscosity<dynamic-value> water, flows easily. Viscosity plays a critical role in processes (injection molding, 3D printing, and fluid transport) in manufacturing. The right viscosity ensures smooth operation, accurate mold filling, and proper material handling. Xometry understands that viscosity is essential for material selection and product design. Selecting materials with the appropriate viscosity ensures the desired flow behavior, proper adhesion, and final product quality, helping Xometry meet specific design requirements and deliver high-performance parts through manufacturing processes . Why is Viscosity Important in Fluids? Viscosity is important in fluids because it determines the internal resistance that controls how easily a substance flows under an applied force. Fluids with low viscosity<dynamic-value> water, move quickly and spread easily, while fluids with high viscosity<dynamic-value> honey, flow slowly and resist motion. The comparison between water and honey demonstrates how viscosity affects flow rate, energy transfer, and surface interaction. Industrial systems depend on viscosity control to maintain performance, reliability, and safety. Viscosity ensures a protective film between mechanical parts to minimize wear and friction under pressure in lubricants. Viscosity regulates application quality, preventing drips, sagging, or uneven spreading in paints and coatings. Engineers and manufacturers rely on precise viscosity measurements to design efficient pumps, cooling systems, and production processes where consistent flow behavior is critical. The control of viscosity ensures predictable outcomes, reduces energy losses, and supports optimal fluid performance in everyday and industrial applications. What are the Factors that Influence Viscosity? The factors that influence viscosity are listed below. Temperature : Viscosity is influenced by temperature because molecular movement changes with heat. Liquid molecules move faster as the temperature rises, reducing internal friction and lowering viscosity. Molecular motion slows at low temperatures, causing an increase in viscosity. Oil thickening during cold weather delays machinery start-up and increases energy use in industrial processes. High viscosity at low temperatures prevents proper mold filling in resin curing or injection molding, producing incomplete or defective products. Pressure : Viscosity increases with rising pressure because molecules are forced closer together, increasing resistance to flow. The effect is more pronounced in liquids with large molecular structures. High pressure can cause lubricants to thicken in manufacturing, reducing flow efficiency. Pressure adjustments are necessary to maintain consistent flow rates and prevent uneven product layers during extrusion or coating processes. Composition : The molecular structure and chemical makeup of a fluid determine its viscosity. Fluids made of large or complex molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, leading to higher viscosity. The formulation of lubricants, paints, and adhesives depends on selecting the right molecular composition to achieve stable performance in industrial production. The ratio of polymers to solvents influences flow, spread, and drying uniformity in paints and coatings. Impurities : Foreign particles or contaminants affect viscosity by disrupting molecular uniformity and increasing internal friction. The presence of solid impurities, moisture, or dissolved gases alters the balance of forces within the fluid. Impurities usually increase viscosity and can block injection nozzles in resin manufacturing. Solvent impurities cause uneven film formation, resulting in sagging, bubbles, or inconsistent finishes in coatings. “Viscosity is at the core of how fluids behave in every manufacturing process. When you understand how a material flows, fills, levels, and transfers energy, you gain control over both performance and quality. The most reliable designs start with respecting the physics of the fluid before shaping the part.” Audrius Zidonis; Principal Engineer at Zidonis Engineering Note from the Editor How is Viscosity Measured in Different Industries? Viscosity is measured by different industries as listed below. Automotive : Automotive industries measure viscosity in lubricants, fuels, and hydraulic fluids using rotational and capillary viscometers, along with cold-cranking simulators for low-temperature performance testing. The instruments determine how fluids behave under varying temperature and shear conditions. Accurate viscosity readings ensure that engine oils maintain flow during cold starts and provide reliable protection under high loads. Consistent viscosity prevents overheating and fluid degradation in brake and transmission systems. Automotive manufacturers rely on viscosity data for certification, quality control, and performance testing to guarantee long-term reliability. Manufacturing : Manufacturers of coatings, paints, adhesives, and resins use flow-cup (efflux time) and rotational viscometry methods. In the flow-cup method, a measured volume of liquid flows through an orifice, and the discharge time is recorded to calculate viscosity. Rotational spindle instruments apply torque at specific shear rates to measure resistance to flow. The tests maintain uniformity in spreadability, film thickness, and curing behavior. Incorrect viscosity levels cause problems (sagging, incomplete mold filling, and uneven surface finishes). Adhesive and sealant plants control viscosity to ensure consistent bonding strength, application ease, and long-term product stability. Pharmaceutica l: Pharmaceutical laboratories use rotational rheometers and capillary viscometers to evaluate the viscosity of syrups, gels, ointments, and injectable solutions. The measurement influences dosage precision, spreadability, and formulation properties that affect bioavailability. Controlled viscosity ensures stability in suspensions and prevents particle settling. Viscosity management guarantees even layering and predictable drug release during tablet coating and formulation. Pharmaceutical manufacturers test viscosity under regulated conditions to meet consistency and safety standards. Food and Beverage : Food and beverage producers measure viscosity to control texture, mouthfeel, and process flow. Instruments such as Brookfield viscometers and falling-ball viscometers assess the viscosity of sauces, creams, and beverages. Viscosity consistency maintains creaminess in dairy products, improves pour behavior in syrups, and improves coating quality in sauces. Food processors track viscosity throughout production to optimize filling, packaging, and storage stability. Polymer and Injection Molding: Polymer and injection molding industries measure the viscosity of resins and molten polymers using high-temperature capillary or rotational rheometers for controlled shear rates. The viscosity behavior at processing temperature determines how effectively the melt fills mold cavities and how uniformly it solidifies. Monitoring viscosity trends allows precise adjustment of processing parameters, improving mold filling, reducing material waste, and preventing product defects. Accurate viscosity control and material selection ensure consistent dimensional stability and surface quality in finished plastic components. What are the Methods for Measuring Viscosity in Industry? The methods for measuring viscosity in industry are listed below. Capillary : The capillary method measures viscosity by recording the time it takes for a fluid to flow through a narrow glass tube under controlled conditions. The measurement depends on tube dimensions, flow time, and fluid density. The method is exact for low- to medium-viscosity fluids (oils, solvents, and fuels). Capillary testing is used to confirm that materials meet flow and temperature performance standards in industrial settings. Quality control laboratories apply the method to detect inconsistencies in fluid formulation, ensuring stable performance during manufacturing and storage. Accurate capillary measurements improve process optimization by identifying variations in raw materials before large-scale production begins. Rotational : The rotational method involves a spindle or rotor immersed in a fluid, where torque is measured as the spindle rotates at a controlled speed. The torque indicates the internal resistance of the fluid, allowing calculation of its dynamic viscosity. The method is used for paints, coatings, adhesives, and lubricants that exhibit non-Newtonian behavior. Rotational viscometry supports quality control by monitoring shear resistance and ensuring consistency across production batches. Manufacturing facilities rely on rotational data to fine-tune mixing speeds, temperature settings, and shear conditions, preventing uneven texture, poor spreadability, or premature curing during processing. Viscometers : Industrial viscometers include instruments like flow-cups, falling-ball viscometers, and vibrating-element devices that measure flow time, fall duration, or vibration damping within a fluid. The instruments are suitable for quick production checks where rapid feedback is essential. Viscometers ensure that liquid products maintain the correct viscosity before packaging or further processing in production lines. Regular use of viscometers in manufacturing helps maintain uniformity across batches, reduce waste, and identify deviations early. Operators maintain consistent texture, stability, and appearance by using continuous viscosity data across multiple production runs. What are the Common Units of Viscosity? The common units of viscosity are listed below. SI Unit (Pa·s) : The pascal-second (Pa·s) is the standard international (SI) unit for measuring dynamic viscosity. One pascal-second corresponds to the viscosity of a fluid in which a shear stress of one pascal produces a shear rate of one reciprocal second (1 s⁻¹). Water at about 20 °C has a viscosity of 0.001 Pa·s, indicating that it flows easily. Industrial fluids such as motor oils have viscosities of 0.1 Pa·s or higher, depending on temperature and formulation. The SI unit of viscosity provides consistency in laboratory and production measurements, ensuring precision in quality control and equipment design. CGS Unit (Poise) : The poise (P) is the unit of dynamic viscosity in the centimeter-gram-second (CGS) system. One poise equals 0.1 Pa·s, and one centipoise (cP) equals 0.001 Pa·s. Water at 20 °C has a viscosity of about 1 cP, while motor oil ranges from 50 cP to 500 cP depending on its grade and temperature. The poise and centipoise are used in engineering and laboratory applications where fine distinctions in fluid viscosities are essential. Consistent use of the units helps manufacturers compare materials, maintain process stability, and ensure uniform fluid behavior during production and testing. How does Viscosity Affect Manufacturing Processes? Viscosity affects manufacturing processes by influencing how fluids flow, spread, coat, and fill, which in turn impacts productivity, quality, and material performance. The viscosity of coolants determines how effectively the coolants carry heat away from the cutting zone and flush out metal particles in machining operations. A moderate increase in coolant viscosity reduces flow through narrow channels, resulting in poorer heat transfer, increased tool wear, and possible thermal damage. Adhesives require a viscosity that allows the material to wet bonding surfaces and fill microscopic voids while maintaining sufficient thickness for structural strength. The adhesive traps air or fails to bond properly if the viscosity is too high, leading to premature failure. Viscosity influences how easily adhesives are mixed, pumped, and dispensed in automated systems. Coatings rely on an appropriate viscosity to enable uniform spreading, controlled film thickness, and prevention of sagging on vertical surfaces. A coating with low viscosity flows off the surface before curing, while one with high viscosity produces uneven layers or texture defects. The viscosity of the molten metal or polymer melt determines how effectively it fills mold cavities and reproduces fine features in casting or injection molding processes. A high-viscosity melt fails to reach thin sections, causing voids or incomplete fills. Viscosity affects how quickly the liquid resin flows and refills beneath each layer in resin-based 3D printing, influencing layer adhesion, print speed, and surface quality. Viscosity has direct relevance for manufacturing consistency and process optimization across all processes. Proper viscosity management ensures uniform outputs, reduces waste and rework, and supports stable process control across production runs. What are the Different Types of Viscosity? The different types of viscosity are listed below. Dynamic Viscosity : Dynamic viscosity measures the internal resistance of a fluid to shear under an applied force. The viscosity formula is defined by the equation μ = τ / γ̇, where μ is dynamic viscosity, τ is shear stress (force per unit area), and γ̇ is shear rate (rate of deformation between fluid layers). Dynamic viscosity is critical in industries such as lubrication, fluid transport, and hydraulics. Viscosity examples include dynamic viscosity, which ensures the fluid maintains a protective film between moving engine parts to reduce wear and friction in motor oils. Higher-viscosity oils can provide better protection at high temperatures, while lower-viscosity oils improve flow and fuel efficiency. Kinematic Viscosity : Kinematic viscosity is the ratio of dynamic viscosity to fluid density, expressed as ν = μ / ρ, where ν is kinematic viscosity, μ is dynamic viscosity, and ρ is fluid density. The property characterizes a fluid’s resistance to flow under its own weight or inertia, independent of external pressure forces. Kinematic viscosity is significant in industries (pipeline transport and coatings), where gravity and inertia influence fluid movement. For example, oil with a higher kinematic viscosity flows more slowly through pipelines, requiring more energy to pump, while in coatings, appropriate kinematic viscosity ensures uniform film formation without drips or uneven coverage. Apparent Viscosity : Apparent viscosity refers to the effective viscosity of a non-Newtonian fluid measured at a specific shear rate, temperature, or other defined condition. The formula is expressed as ηₐₚₚ = τ / γ̇, where ηₐₚₚ is apparent viscosity, τ is shear stress (force per unit area), and γ̇ is shear rate (rate of deformation). Apparent viscosity is used to characterize materials (adhesives, paints, and polymer melts) whose viscosity changes with shear rate during processing. For example, the apparent viscosity of a resin affects how it flows and adheres during layer deposition in 3D printing, influencing print quality and speed. What is Dynamic Viscosity? Dynamic viscosity is a measure of a fluid’s internal resistance to shear under an applied force. Dynamic viscosity relates the shear stress exerted on the fluid to the resulting rate of deformation between adjacent layers. Fluid flow becomes sluggish and requires greater energy input to maintain movement when dynamic viscosity is high. Appropriate dynamic viscosity helps maintain a stable thin film of lubricant between moving parts and prevents direct metal-to-metal contact in applications such as engine lubrication, injection molding , and industrial machinery, thereby reducing wear. The lubricant film breaks down and causes damage if the dynamic viscosity is too low. The fluid does not circulate efficiently if the dynamic viscosity is too high, increasing drag, pump load, and energy consumption. What is Kinematic Viscosity? Kinematic viscosity is a measure of a fluid’s inherent resistance to flow relative to its density. Kinematic viscosity is calculated by dividing a fluid’s dynamic viscosity by its density (ν = μ / ρ). A fluid's kinematic viscosity indicates how easily it moves under its own mass per unit volume compared with its internal resistance to flow. Fuel flow systems use it for consistent delivery, coolant circulation systems for reliable channel traversal, and manufacturing fluid transport processes where gravity and inertia influence throughput and stability. What is Apparent Viscosity? Apparent viscosity is the effective measure of a fluid’s resistance to shear under specific processing conditions (defined shear rate, temperature, or applied stress). Apparent viscosity describes how a fluid’s internal structure responds when adjacent layers move at different rates. Non-Newtonian fluids have a variable apparent viscosity depending on the shear rate or applied stress. For example, coatings must have a lower apparent viscosity under high shear during spraying for easy application and a higher apparent viscosity at rest to prevent sagging. Sealants require an apparent viscosity that allows them to flow into joints and then stabilize to remain in place. Apparent viscosity determines how readily the material flows under high shear during extrusion and how well it maintains shape after exiting the die in polymer extrusion. Proper control of apparent viscosity ensures uniform products, efficient processing, and minimal defects in manufacturing. How does Viscosity Affect Injection Molding Processes? Viscosity affects the injection molding process by determining how easily the resin flows into the mold, how it cools, and the final part quality. High-viscosity resins flow more slowly, which leads to incomplete filling or short shots in intricate or thin-walled sections. Higher injection pressures are required, which increases overall cycle time. Resins with excessively low viscosity can leak into parting lines, create flash, or reduce dimensional accuracy. Proper viscosity ensures that the mold fills, cools evenly, and produces parts with smooth surfaces, minimal sink marks, and strong weld lines. Expertise in material selection helps balance viscosity for optimal mold filling, cooling, and part quality. How does Viscosity Impact Extrusion Processes? Viscosity impacts polymer extrusion by governing how the melt flows, stabilizes, and forms the final product dimensions. High-viscosity melts resist flow, requiring more force to push material through the screw and die, which reduces production rates. Lower-viscosity melts flow more easily and increase throughput, but lead to unstable flow, uneven wall thickness, or surface defects. Fluctuations in melt viscosity in non-Newtonian polymers cause pressure variations that affect dimensional consistency and product quality. Precise control of viscosity ensures uniform die filling, consistent cross-sections, and proper cooling. Real-time monitoring of melt viscosity allows adjustments to screw speed, temperature, and back-pressure, making viscosity a critical factor for quality control and process optimization in extrusion. What is the Importance of Viscosity in Casting? The importance of viscosity in casting is listed below. Flow into Mold Cavities : Viscosity determines how easily molten metal or ceramic slurry penetrates mold geometry. High viscosity or insufficiently heated metal prevents full filling of thin sections, leading to voids or incomplete castings. Defect Prevention : Maintaining proper viscosity reduces defects such as porosity, surface roughness, and, in investment casting, shell cracking and incomplete shell formation. Stable viscosity ensures uniform shell thickness and reliable strength. Die Casting Relevance : The molten alloy must flow rapidly into the mold before solidification begins in die casting. Lower viscosity improves mold filling, reduces cold shuts, and increases part quality. Investment Casting Relevance : The viscosity of the ceramic slurry affects coating layers on the wax pattern, shell integrity, and final casting accuracy in investment casting. Maintaining optimal viscosity ensures proper coating, mold strength, and dimensional precision. How does Viscosity Influence 3D Printing (Additive Manufacturing)? Viscosity influences 3D printing processes by governing how well the material flows, how each layer adheres, and how the final structure maintains its shape. Stereolithography (SLA) requires low-viscosity resin to refill the tank rapidly between layers, reduce trapped air or voids, and enable fine feature resolution. The viscosity of molten polymer affects flow through the nozzle, filament bonding, and layer consistency, directly impacting print precision, strength, and quality in Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM). Powder-bed processes such as Selective Laser Sintering (SLS) depend on the flow behavior of the partially melted powder to ensure particles coalesce properly, which affects density, mechanical strength, and dimensional accuracy. Proper control of viscosity across the processes ensures high print precision, strong interlayer adhesion, and superior structural integrity in printed parts. Why is Viscosity Important in Coatings and Paint Formulations? Viscosity is essential in coatings and paint formulations because it controls how the liquid flows onto and adheres to a surface. Proper viscosity improves sprayability, film formation, and drying behavior in industrial paints and powder coatings. Low viscosity increases atomization during spray application, permitting fine mist formation and even coverage. High viscosity supports a thicker film build without sagging on vertical surfaces, provided it remains within the application range. Maintaining optimal viscosity in paint lines ensures a consistent surface finish, accurate film thickness, and defect-free drying. Powder coatings benefit from controlling melt viscosity during curing to ensure proper flow, leveling, and uniform protective layers. Insufficient viscosity control results in uneven coatings, runs, orange peel texture, and reduced durability of the finished product. How does Viscosity Affect the Performance of Adhesives and Sealants? Viscosity affects the performance of adhesives and sealants by controlling how well the material flows, wets the substrate, and forms a strong bond, and how easily it is applied. Proper viscosity ensures the adhesive penetrates surface irregularities and establishes intimate contact between surfaces. Lower viscosity adhesives flow readily, filling micro‑voids on rough or porous surfaces and improving bond strength. Higher viscosity adhesives remain in place under gravity or vertical orientation, preserving joint thickness and preventing sagging or dripping during application. The viscosity of epoxy resins influences mixing, dispensing, and layer uniformity, affecting cohesive strength upon curing. Sealant viscosity determines how well the material extrudes into joints and gaps and how well it resists movement under load after curing. Deviations from the optimal viscosity range reduce bond strength, impair gap-filling, or compromise joint integrity. Why Do Lubricants in Machining Depend on Viscosity? Lubricants in machining depend on viscosity because it determines the thickness of the protective film between moving parts, reducing wear, friction, and heat generation. Correct viscosity ensures the film remains stable under load, preventing metal‑to‑metal contact. The lubricant is unable to form a sufficient film if the viscosity is too low, increasing friction and wear. Excessively high viscosity impedes fluid flow and reduces cooling efficiency, increasing localized heat. Viscosity influences chip removal and tool friction in Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machining by controlling how well the lubricant or coolant reaches the cutting interface. Proper viscosity ensures adequate lubrication of critical components in automotive engines, increasing performance and prolonging engine life. What are Real-World Applications of Viscosity in Manufacturing? The real-world applications of viscosity in manufacturing are listed below. Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 22 min read Published December 4, 2025 Updated August 26, 2026 Viscosity is the measure of a fluid’s resistance to flow. Viscosity definition indicates how thick or thin a fluid is and determines how easily it flows under an applied force. A fluid with high viscosity<dynamic-value> honey, flows slowly, while a fluid with low viscosity<dynamic-value> water, flows easily. Viscosity plays a critical role in processes (injection molding, 3D printing, and fluid transport) in manufacturing. The right viscosity ensures smooth operation, accurate mold filling, and proper material handling. Xometry understands that viscosity is essential for material selection and product design. Selecting materials with the appropriate viscosity ensures the desired flow behavior, proper adhesion, and final product quality, helping Xometry meet specific design requirements and deliver high-performance parts through manufacturing processes . Why is Viscosity Important in Fluids? Viscosity is important in fluids because it determines the internal resistance that controls how easily a substance flows under an applied force. Fluids with low viscosity<dynamic-value> water, move quickly and spread easily, while fluids with high viscosity<dynamic-value> honey, flow slowly and resist motion. The comparison between water and honey demonstrates how viscosity affects flow rate, energy transfer, and surface interaction. Industrial systems depend on viscosity control to maintain performance, reliability, and safety. Viscosity ensures a protective film between mechanical parts to minimize wear and friction under pressure in lubricants. Viscosity regulates application quality, preventing drips, sagging, or uneven spreading in paints and coatings. Engineers and manufacturers rely on precise viscosity measurements to design efficient pumps, cooling systems, and production processes where consistent flow behavior is critical. The control of viscosity ensures predictable outcomes, reduces energy losses, and supports optimal fluid performance in everyday and industrial applications. What are the Factors that Influence Viscosity? The factors that influence viscosity are listed below. Temperature : Viscosity is influenced by temperature because molecular movement changes with heat. Liquid molecules move faster as the temperature rises, reducing internal friction and lowering viscosity. Molecular motion slows at low temperatures, causing an increase in viscosity. Oil thickening during cold weather delays machinery start-up and increases energy use in industrial processes. High viscosity at low temperatures prevents proper mold filling in resin curing or injection molding, producing incomplete or defective products. Pressure : Viscosity increases with rising pressure because molecules are forced closer together, increasing resistance to flow. The effect is more pronounced in liquids with large molecular structures. High pressure can cause lubricants to thicken in manufacturing, reducing flow efficiency. Pressure adjustments are necessary to maintain consistent flow rates and prevent uneven product layers during extrusion or coating processes. Composition : The molecular structure and chemical makeup of a fluid determine its viscosity. Fluids made of large or complex molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, leading to higher viscosity. The formulation of lubricants, paints, and adhesives depends on selecting the right molecular composition to achieve stable performance in industrial production. The ratio of polymers to solvents influences flow, spread, and drying uniformity in paints and coatings. Impurities : Foreign particles or contaminants affect viscosity by disrupting molecular uniformity and increasing internal friction. The presence of solid impurities, moisture, or dissolved gases alters the balance of forces within the fluid. Impurities usually increase viscosity and can block injection nozzles in resin manufacturing. Solvent impurities cause uneven film formation, resulting in sagging, bubbles, or inconsistent finishes in coatings. “Viscosity is at the core of how fluids behave in every manufacturing process. When you understand how a material flows, fills, levels, and transfers energy, you gain control over both performance and quality. The most reliable designs start with respecting the physics of the fluid before shaping the part.” Audrius Zidonis; Principal Engineer at Zidonis Engineering Note from the Editor How is Viscosity Measured in Different Industries? Viscosity is measured by different industries as listed below. Automotive : Automotive industries measure viscosity in lubricants, fuels, and hydraulic fluids using rotational and capillary viscometers, along with cold-cranking simulators for low-temperature performance testing. The instruments determine how fluids behave under varying temperature and shear conditions. Accurate viscosity readings ensure that engine oils maintain flow during cold starts and provide reliable protection under high loads. Consistent viscosity prevents overheating and fluid degradation in brake and transmission systems. Automotive manufacturers rely on viscosity data for certification, quality control, and performance testing to guarantee long-term reliability. Manufacturing : Manufacturers of coatings, paints, adhesives, and resins use flow-cup (efflux time) and rotational viscometry methods. In the flow-cup method, a measured volume of liquid flows through an orifice, and the discharge time is recorded to calculate viscosity. Rotational spindle instruments apply torque at specific shear rates to measure resistance to flow. The tests maintain uniformity in spreadability, film thickness, and curing behavior. Incorrect viscosity levels cause problems (sagging, incomplete mold filling, and uneven surface finishes). Adhesive and sealant plants control viscosity to ensure consistent bonding strength, application ease, and long-term product stability. Pharmaceutica l: Pharmaceutical laboratories use rotational rheometers and capillary viscometers to evaluate the viscosity of syrups, gels, ointments, and injectable solutions. The measurement influences dosage precision, spreadability, and formulation properties that affect bioavailability. Controlled viscosity ensures stability in suspensions and prevents particle settling. Viscosity management guarantees even layering and predictable drug release during tablet coating and formulation. Pharmaceutical manufacturers test viscosity under regulated conditions to meet consistency and safety standards. Food and Beverage : Food and beverage producers measure viscosity to control texture, mouthfeel, and process flow. Instruments such as Brookfield viscometers and falling-ball viscometers assess the viscosity of sauces, creams, and beverages. Viscosity consistency maintains creaminess in dairy products, improves pour behavior in syrups, and improves coating quality in sauces. Food processors track viscosity throughout production to optimize filling, packaging, and storage stability. Polymer and Injection Molding: Polymer and injection molding industries measure the viscosity of resins and molten polymers using high-temperature capillary or rotational rheometers for controlled shear rates. The viscosity behavior at processing temperature determines how effectively the melt fills mold cavities and how uniformly it solidifies. Monitoring viscosity trends allows precise adjustment of processing parameters, improving mold filling, reducing material waste, and preventing product defects. Accurate viscosity control and material selection ensure consistent dimensional stability and surface quality in finished plastic components. What are the Methods for Measuring Viscosity in Industry? The methods for measuring viscosity in industry are listed below. Capillary : The capillary method measures viscosity by recording the time it takes for a fluid to flow through a narrow glass tube under controlled conditions. The measurement depends on tube dimensions, flow time, and fluid density. The method is exact for low- to medium-viscosity fluids (oils, solvents, and fuels). Capillary testing is used to confirm that materials meet flow and temperature performance standards in industrial settings. Quality control laboratories apply the method to detect inconsistencies in fluid formulation, ensuring stable performance during manufacturing and storage. Accurate capillary measurements improve process optimization by identifying variations in raw materials before large-scale production begins. Rotational : The rotational method involves a spindle or rotor immersed in a fluid, where torque is measured as the spindle rotates at a controlled speed. The torque indicates the internal resistance of the fluid, allowing calculation of its dynamic viscosity. The method is used for paints, coatings, adhesives, and lubricants that exhibit non-Newtonian behavior. Rotational viscometry supports quality control by monitoring shear resistance and ensuring consistency across production batches. Manufacturing facilities rely on rotational data to fine-tune mixing speeds, temperature settings, and shear conditions, preventing uneven texture, poor spreadability, or premature curing during processing. Viscometers : Industrial viscometers include instruments like flow-cups, falling-ball viscometers, and vibrating-element devices that measure flow time, fall duration, or vibration damping within a fluid. The instruments are suitable for quick production checks where rapid feedback is essential. Viscometers ensure that liquid products maintain the correct viscosity before packaging or further processing in production lines. Regular use of viscometers in manufacturing helps maintain uniformity across batches, reduce waste, and identify deviations early. Operators maintain consistent texture, stability, and appearance by using continuous viscosity data across multiple production runs. What are the Common Units of Viscosity? The common units of viscosity are listed below. SI Unit (Pa·s) : The pascal-second (Pa·s) is the standard international (SI) unit for measuring dynamic viscosity. One pascal-second corresponds to the viscosity of a fluid in which a shear stress of one pascal produces a shear rate of one reciprocal second (1 s⁻¹). Water at about 20 °C has a viscosity of 0.001 Pa·s, indicating that it flows easily. Industrial fluids such as motor oils have viscosities of 0.1 Pa·s or higher, depending on temperature and formulation. The SI unit of viscosity provides consistency in laboratory and production measurements, ensuring precision in quality control and equipment design. CGS Unit (Poise) : The poise (P) is the unit of dynamic viscosity in the centimeter-gram-second (CGS) system. One poise equals 0.1 Pa·s, and one centipoise (cP) equals 0.001 Pa·s. Water at 20 °C has a viscosity of about 1 cP, while motor oil ranges from 50 cP to 500 cP depending on its grade and temperature. The poise and centipoise are used in engineering and laboratory applications where fine distinctions in fluid viscosities are essential. Consistent use of the units helps manufacturers compare materials, maintain process stability, and ensure uniform fluid behavior during production and testing. How does Viscosity Affect Manufacturing Processes? Viscosity affects manufacturing processes by influencing how fluids flow, spread, coat, and fill, which in turn impacts productivity, quality, and material performance. The viscosity of coolants determines how effectively the coolants carry heat away from the cutting zone and flush out metal particles in machining operations. A moderate increase in coolant viscosity reduces flow through narrow channels, resulting in poorer heat transfer, increased tool wear, and possible thermal damage. Adhesives require a viscosity that allows the material to wet bonding surfaces and fill microscopic voids while maintaining sufficient thickness for structural strength. The adhesive traps air or fails to bond properly if the viscosity is too high, leading to premature failure. Viscosity influences how easily adhesives are mixed, pumped, and dispensed in automated systems. Coatings rely on an appropriate viscosity to enable uniform spreading, controlled film thickness, and prevention of sagging on vertical surfaces. A coating with low viscosity flows off the surface before curing, while one with high viscosity produces uneven layers or texture defects. The viscosity of the molten metal or polymer melt determines how effectively it fills mold cavities and reproduces fine features in casting or injection molding processes. A high-viscosity melt fails to reach thin sections, causing voids or incomplete fills. Viscosity affects how quickly the liquid resin flows and refills beneath each layer in resin-based 3D printing, influencing layer adhesion, print speed, and surface quality. Viscosity has direct relevance for manufacturing consistency and process optimization across all processes. Proper viscosity management ensures uniform outputs, reduces waste and rework, and supports stable process control across production runs. What are the Different Types of Viscosity? The different types of viscosity are listed below. Dynamic Viscosity : Dynamic viscosity measures the internal resistance of a fluid to shear under an applied force. The viscosity formula is defined by the equation μ = τ / γ̇, where μ is dynamic viscosity, τ is shear stress (force per unit area), and γ̇ is shear rate (rate of deformation between fluid layers). Dynamic viscosity is critical in industries such as lubrication, fluid transport, and hydraulics. Viscosity examples include dynamic viscosity, which ensures the fluid maintains a protective film between moving engine parts to reduce wear and friction in motor oils. Higher-viscosity oils can provide better protection at high temperatures, while lower-viscosity oils improve flow and fuel efficiency. Kinematic Viscosity : Kinematic viscosity is the ratio of dynamic viscosity to fluid density, expressed as ν = μ / ρ, where ν is kinematic viscosity, μ is dynamic viscosity, and ρ is fluid density. The property characterizes a fluid’s resistance to flow under its own weight or inertia, independent of external pressure forces. Kinematic viscosity is significant in industries (pipeline transport and coatings), where gravity and inertia influence fluid movement. For example, oil with a higher kinematic viscosity flows more slowly through pipelines, requiring more energy to pump, while in coatings, appropriate kinematic viscosity ensures uniform film formation without drips or uneven coverage. Apparent Viscosity : Apparent viscosity refers to the effective viscosity of a non-Newtonian fluid measured at a specific shear rate, temperature, or other defined condition. The formula is expressed as ηₐₚₚ = τ / γ̇, where ηₐₚₚ is apparent viscosity, τ is shear stress (force per unit area), and γ̇ is shear rate (rate of deformation). Apparent viscosity is used to characterize materials (adhesives, paints, and polymer melts) whose viscosity changes with shear rate during processing. For example, the apparent viscosity of a resin affects how it flows and adheres during layer deposition in 3D printing, influencing print quality and speed. What is Dynamic Viscosity? Dynamic viscosity is a measure of a fluid’s internal resistance to shear under an applied force. Dynamic viscosity relates the shear stress exerted on the fluid to the resulting rate of deformation between adjacent layers. Fluid flow becomes sluggish and requires greater energy input to maintain movement when dynamic viscosity is high. Appropriate dynamic viscosity helps maintain a stable thin film of lubricant between moving parts and prevents direct metal-to-metal contact in applications such as engine lubrication, injection molding , and industrial machinery, thereby reducing wear. The lubricant film breaks down and causes damage if the dynamic viscosity is too low. The fluid does not circulate efficiently if the dynamic viscosity is too high, increasing drag, pump load, and energy consumption. What is Kinematic Viscosity? Kinematic viscosity is a measure of a fluid’s inherent resistance to flow relative to its density. Kinematic viscosity is calculated by dividing a fluid’s dynamic viscosity by its density (ν = μ / ρ). A fluid's kinematic viscosity indicates how easily it moves under its own mass per unit volume compared with its internal resistance to flow. Fuel flow systems use it for consistent delivery, coolant circulation systems for reliable channel traversal, and manufacturing fluid transport processes where gravity and inertia influence throughput and stability. What is Apparent Viscosity? Apparent viscosity is the effective measure of a fluid’s resistance to shear under specific processing conditions (defined shear rate, temperature, or applied stress). Apparent viscosity describes how a fluid’s internal structure responds when adjacent layers move at different rates. Non-Newtonian fluids have a variable apparent viscosity depending on the shear rate or applied stress. For example, coatings must have a lower apparent viscosity under high shear during spraying for easy application and a higher apparent viscosity at rest to prevent sagging. Sealants require an apparent viscosity that allows them to flow into joints and then stabilize to remain in place. Apparent viscosity determines how readily the material flows under high shear during extrusion and how well it maintains shape after exiting the die in polymer extrusion. Proper control of apparent viscosity ensures uniform products, efficient processing, and minimal defects in manufacturing. How does Viscosity Affect Injection Molding Processes? Viscosity affects the injection molding process by determining how easily the resin flows into the mold, how it cools, and the final part quality. High-viscosity resins flow more slowly, which leads to incomplete filling or short shots in intricate or thin-walled sections. Higher injection pressures are required, which increases overall cycle time. Resins with excessively low viscosity can leak into parting lines, create flash, or reduce dimensional accuracy. Proper viscosity ensures that the mold fills, cools evenly, and produces parts with smooth surfaces, minimal sink marks, and strong weld lines. Expertise in material selection helps balance viscosity for optimal mold filling, cooling, and part quality. How does Viscosity Impact Extrusion Processes? Viscosity impacts polymer extrusion by governing how the melt flows, stabilizes, and forms the final product dimensions. High-viscosity melts resist flow, requiring more force to push material through the screw and die, which reduces production rates. Lower-viscosity melts flow more easily and increase throughput, but lead to unstable flow, uneven wall thickness, or surface defects. Fluctuations in melt viscosity in non-Newtonian polymers cause pressure variations that affect dimensional consistency and product quality. Precise control of viscosity ensures uniform die filling, consistent cross-sections, and proper cooling. Real-time monitoring of melt viscosity allows adjustments to screw speed, temperature, and back-pressure, making viscosity a critical factor for quality control and process optimization in extrusion. What is the Importance of Viscosity in Casting? The importance of viscosity in casting is listed below. Flow into Mold Cavities : Viscosity determines how easily molten metal or ceramic slurry penetrates mold geometry. High viscosity or insufficiently heated metal prevents full filling of thin sections, leading to voids or incomplete castings. Defect Prevention : Maintaining proper viscosity reduces defects such as porosity, surface roughness, and, in investment casting, shell cracking and incomplete shell formation. Stable viscosity ensures uniform shell thickness and reliable strength. Die Casting Relevance : The molten alloy must flow rapidly into the mold before solidification begins in die casting. Lower viscosity improves mold filling, reduces cold shuts, and increases part quality. Investment Casting Relevance : The viscosity of the ceramic slurry affects coating layers on the wax pattern, shell integrity, and final casting accuracy in investment casting. Maintaining optimal viscosity ensures proper coating, mold strength, and dimensional precision. How does Viscosity Influence 3D Printing (Additive Manufacturing)? Viscosity influences 3D printing processes by governing how well the material flows, how each layer adheres, and how the final structure maintains its shape. Stereolithography (SLA) requires low-viscosity resin to refill the tank rapidly between layers, reduce trapped air or voids, and enable fine feature resolution. The viscosity of molten polymer affects flow through the nozzle, filament bonding, and layer consistency, directly impacting print precision, strength, and quality in Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM). Powder-bed processes such as Selective Laser Sintering (SLS) depend on the flow behavior of the partially melted powder to ensure particles coalesce properly, which affects density, mechanical strength, and dimensional accuracy. Proper control of viscosity across the processes ensures high print precision, strong interlayer adhesion, and superior structural integrity in printed parts. Why is Viscosity Important in Coatings and Paint Formulations? Viscosity is essential in coatings and paint formulations because it controls how the liquid flows onto and adheres to a surface. Proper viscosity improves sprayability, film formation, and drying behavior in industrial paints and powder coatings. Low viscosity increases atomization during spray application, permitting fine mist formation and even coverage. High viscosity supports a thicker film build without sagging on vertical surfaces, provided it remains within the application range. Maintaining optimal viscosity in paint lines ensures a consistent surface finish, accurate film thickness, and defect-free drying. Powder coatings benefit from controlling melt viscosity during curing to ensure proper flow, leveling, and uniform protective layers. Insufficient viscosity control results in uneven coatings, runs, orange peel texture, and reduced durability of the finished product. How does Viscosity Affect the Performance of Adhesives and Sealants? Viscosity affects the performance of adhesives and sealants by controlling how well the material flows, wets the substrate, and forms a strong bond, and how easily it is applied. Proper viscosity ensures the adhesive penetrates surface irregularities and establishes intimate contact between surfaces. Lower viscosity adhesives flow readily, filling micro‑voids on rough or porous surfaces and improving bond strength. Higher viscosity adhesives remain in place under gravity or vertical orientation, preserving joint thickness and preventing sagging or dripping during application. The viscosity of epoxy resins influences mixing, dispensing, and layer uniformity, affecting cohesive strength upon curing. Sealant viscosity determines how well the material extrudes into joints and gaps and how well it resists movement under load after curing. Deviations from the optimal viscosity range reduce bond strength, impair gap-filling, or compromise joint integrity. Why Do Lubricants in Machining Depend on Viscosity? Correct viscosity ensures the film remains stable under load, preventing metal‑to‑metal contact. The lubricant is unable to form a sufficient film if the viscosity is too low, increasing friction and wear. Excessively high viscosity impedes fluid flow and reduces cooling efficiency, increasing localized heat. Viscosity influences chip removal and tool friction in Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machining by controlling how well the lubricant or coolant reaches the cutting interface. Proper viscosity ensures adequate lubrication of critical components in automotive engines, increasing performance and prolonging engine life. events.before: Resources / Sheet / Understanding Sheet Metal Tolerances Understanding Sheet Metal Tolerances Written by Greg Paulsen 2 min read Published October 6, 2020 Updated August 21, 2026 Check out our list of quick tips and tolerance specifications for designing Sheet Metal countersinks, curls, and hems! A Quick Guide to Countersinks, Curls, and Hems Compared to other machining processes, designing Sheet Metal parts is relatively straight-forward. Sheet metal parts are made from a single metal sheet by punching, cutting, stamping, and/or bending and are known for their end-use durability. But there are still many important design-for-manufacturability issues to consider. Check out our list of quick tips and tolerance specifications for designing Sheet Metal countersinks, curls, and hems! And for even more information, download our free Sheet Metal Design Guide ! Countersinks The maximum depth of a countersink is .6 times the material thickness of the part. Countersinks must be at least 8 times the material thickness from each other, 4 times the material’s thickness from an edge, and 3 times the material’s thickness from a bend. Curls Outside radius of curls must be at least 2 times the material’s thickness. Holes should be placed away from the curl at least a distance of the radius of the curl plus the material’s thickness. Bends should be at least 6 times the material’s thickness plus the radius of the curl. Hems Hems are folds to the edge of a part to create a rounded, safe edge. Hems may be open, flat, or tear-dropped, and tolerances depend on the hem’s radius, material thickness, and features near the hem (Note: flat hems risk fracturing the material at the bend and should be avoided if possible). For open hems, minimum inside diameter is equal to the material thickness (larger diameters tend to lose circular shape), and the return length is at least 4 times the material’s thickness. Tear-dropped hems must maintain an inside diameter of at least one material’s thickness, an opening of at least ¼ the material’s thickness, and return length is also 4 times the material’s thickness. events.before: Resources / Supplier Shop Tips / Tapping Away: Common Problems, Causes, and Corrections for Taps and Tap Sets Tapping Away: Common Problems, Causes, and Corrections for Taps and Tap Sets Written by Team Xometry 7 min read Published September 18, 2020 Updated August 21, 2026 From breakage to loading, and galling to rough threads, we’ve got some answers that could save you some serious frustration and keep broken taps from breaking your bank. Tapping is one of the machining types most prone to issues because it requires careful balance, planning, and research . Especially when you’re using a CNC machine, lack of sensory connection to the tapping operation can mean that you might miss issues until they’re too late to correct. Because tapping is also one of the last operations to be performed on a part, screwing it up can result in a whole lot of scrapped parts and wasted time. From breakage to loading, and galling to rough threads, we’ve got some answers that could save you some serious frustration and keep broken taps from breaking your bank. First Issue: Tap Breakage By far, the most obvious sign of an issue is tap breakage. If your tool is breaking, cracking, or chipping, you need to administer some TLC quickly. First, just double check that you’re using a machine with the correct power output, and tool. If your tool geometry is off, or the tap isn’t the correct hardness for the use case, you’re fighting a losing battle. Also, make sure the tap is sharp. If you’re working with a dull tap, you maybe have one or two sharpens before you should get yourself a replacement . Also, try not to let your tap get too dull before resharpening. Since dull tools can also cause work hardening (also a cause of breakage), you have extra incentive to stay on the up and up with your tool maintenance. Similarly, you can reduce issues by making sure you’ve got the right grind on your tap. A proper cutting angle and chamfer angle ensure good work. Also often overlooked in tapping is the quality of the hole itself. If your drilled hole is too shallow or too small, you’re either going to ruin the tool or the workpiece with shoddy work. Keep in mind that drill size does not always equal hole size. Checking that the entire process is solid — not just the tool — is essential. If your drilled hole is too shallow for the tap you’re using, that’s going to cause issues as well. Either adjust your drilled hole or the length of your chamfer. Similarly, if your drilled hole and your tap are misaligned — even by a frog hair — your tap is at risk of damage. Honestly, this is the number one reason for tap breakage. Misalignment by even a fraction will be magnified the further the process is pushed, and doubly cause screw-ups (see what I did there?) when your tap reverses from the hole. Misalignment-related breakage is also caused by using incorrect holding devices. Check that the holding device you are using is correct for alignment with the hole. Lastly, you might not be applying the right kind of lubrication — and I don’t mean bribe money or bourbon (though we wouldn’t personally refuse either)*. If you’re experiencing breakage, chipping, or fracturing, you may need to reduce the friction on your tap by increasing the amount of lubrication during machining. You may need to switch the type of lubrication you’re using — a purpose-made tapping lubricant is your best bet. Better lubrication also improves chip removal. This is definitely one area where more is more. *I’m joking. Or am I? Try Xometry's Instant Quoting Engine® Test-drive a sample part to get instant pricing and DFM analysis Launch Demo Second Issue: Tap Failure on Reversal When your tap craps out during reversal, it might be because it’s cutting too tightly. Check that your cutting angle isn’t too small, and increase it if necessary. Galling is a possible player here as well. Basically, when your threads gall, the pressure, and friction between material and tap are high enough that some of the material is pulled along as the tap moves. That’s some pretty unfortunate physics. You can reduce pressure by decreasing the thread percentage you’re trying to cut at, and increasing your land(s) width. The face angle on the back of the land is often the main culprit in this case. If your tap is stalling on reversal, the cause is likely chips jamming too tightly in the tap flutes. You should try to avoid this at all costs since it can quickly ruin your work or break your tap. If your chips aren’t forming and evacuating right, it might call for a different type of tap, with more generous chamfers or a cutting angle better suited to the material or project. As usual, also keep an eye on the lubrication type and amount you’re providing. Don’t skimp! Another possibility is that your flutes are ground incorrectly. If your flute geometry is wrong for the workpiece material, chip evacuation is going to be a whole mess. Third Issue: Stripped or Chipped Tap Threads If you’re having issues with stripped or chipped threads, it’s most likely that your tap and hole are not properly aligned. Even a slight misalignment can increase pressure and friction greatly. Check your tap holder and machine are right for the job, and possibly look into chamfering the hole before you try to use a tap on it. Also, make sure to check the tap alignment from several perspectives before you go ahead and start machining. Stripping can also be caused by a dull or worn tap, which is also an issue that might “work harden” your workpiece. Sadly, trying to tap work-hardened material may also cause your tap to chip, which makes this issue a bit of a vicious circle. A poorly sharpened tap might produce similar results, so it’s sometimes better to replace a tool rather than risk ruining your work. Chipping is also a symptom of poor handling. Taps have to be much harder than the materials they are cutting, but this additional hardness also makes them brittle and prone to chipping. Handle with care! If you’re nice to your tools, they’ll be nice to you right back. Your surface treatment can also make a whole world of difference when it comes to tap effectiveness and wear. Different coatings are optimal at different temperatures, and ideal for different workpiece types. Finding the correct combination of coating, tool geometry, and tapping speed is a tricky balance, but a worthwhile line to walk. Shop affordable Taps and Tap Sets at Xometry Supplies Shop Now Fourth Issue: Torn Threads in Tapped Part Torn threads are just about the biggest letdown after stripped threads. If your tap is tearing or pulling the metal as it turns, the issue is most likely that your speed is too low. You may also need to sharpen or replace your tap. Be sure that your tap doesn’t have broken threads itself, as that’s a problem for obvious reasons. The amount and kind of lubricant you’re using is also an important factor. Make sure you’re not being stingy, and are using an ideal lubricant for your use-type. Lastly, check that chips aren’t clogging up your flute and mucking up your machining. Torn threads might also happen if your cutting face angle is too small. The cutting face angle is largely responsible for reducing impact load, as well as managing chip formation and evacuation. Slight differences in the cutting face geometry of your taps can take your part quality up several notches. You also might need to check the size of the hole you’re drilling in comparison to the size of your tap . It could very well be the case that your tap drill is too small. This isn’t an uncommon problem, but it is an important one to get straight. The fight here is thread strength (i.e., enough material) vs. reasonable torque (i.e., bigger hole/tap ratio). If you’re getting pulled and torn threads, you probably need to reevaluate the relationship between your hole and tap, specifically to reduce torque. Depending on your needs, increase your tap drill size to create a larger hole, or possibly reduce your tap size.
